teile.einleitung: The giant panda is a black and white bear from China. It eats almost nothing but bamboo and spends most of the day eating. It is the emblem of the conservation organisation WWF.
wichtigste: The giant panda lives in cool, damp mountain forests in China.
It eats almost nothing but bamboo.
It often eats for more than ten hours a day.
A thumb-like bone helps it to hold the bamboo.
It does not hibernate.
A baby panda weighs only about 100 grams at birth.

abschnitte.text: The giant panda belongs to the family of **bears**. Its fur is **black and white**. Black are the ears, the legs, the shoulders and the patches around the eyes. It lives in **mountain forests** in the interior of China, where it is cool and damp and a lot of bamboo grows. Unlike many other bears, it **does not hibernate**. Even in winter it searches for bamboo.

The panda eats almost nothing but **bamboo**, that is, leaves, stems and young shoots. Bamboo, however, provides little energy. That is why the panda has to eat a great deal of it. It often eats for **more than ten hours** a day. The rest of the time it mostly rests, to save energy.

On its front paw the panda has an **extended bone** at the wrist. It works like an extra **thumb**. With it the panda can hold bamboo stems skilfully. With its strong teeth and jaws it also bites through tough stems.

A newborn panda weighs only about **100 grams**, as much as a bar of chocolate. It is pink, almost naked and blind. The mother looks after her young for many months. Only gradually does it get its typical black and white fur. A grown-up panda, on the other hand, becomes much heavier than a person.

Since it was founded in **1961**, the **WWF** has had a giant panda in its emblem. The WWF was founded in Switzerland. For a long time the panda was seriously threatened because its forests were being cut down. China has created many **protected areas**. Since then the number of wild pandas has increased again.

gewusst: A baby panda is about a thousand times lighter than its mother at birth.
The WWF has its seat in Gland in the canton of Vaud.

teile.einleitung: The Hawaiian Islands lie in the middle of the Pacific and belong to the USA. They were formed from volcanoes that erupted on the seabed. Some of these volcanoes are still active today and let the islands keep growing.
wichtigste: The Hawaiian Islands were formed from volcanoes in the sea.
They lie in the middle of the Pacific, far from the mainland.
Hawaii is a US state and the only one that consists only of islands.
Kilauea is one of the most active volcanoes in the world.
Mauna Loa is the biggest active volcano on Earth.
Mauna Kea is over 10,000 metres high measured from the seabed.
In the legends, Pele is the goddess of volcanoes.

abschnitte.text: On the seabed, **volcanoes** erupted again and again over a long time. The **lava** piled up, layer upon layer, until the mountains stuck out of the water. This is how the Hawaiian Islands formed. When lava flows into the sea today, it cools in the water and becomes new rock. So the island gets **bigger** bit by bit.

Hawaii lies in the middle of the **Pacific Ocean**. The islands are very far from any mainland. Hawaii is a **US state**. It is the only state that consists only of islands. Because of its remote location, there are many plants and animals there that occur nowhere else.

On the big island of Hawaii stand enormous volcanoes. **Kilauea** is one of the most active volcanoes in the world and lies in **Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park**. **Mauna Loa** is a huge **shield volcano**. Measured by its mass, it is the biggest active volcano on Earth. **Mauna Kea** rises over 4000 metres out of the sea. Measured from the seabed, it is even over **10,000 metres** high.

In the old legends of Hawaii there is the goddess **Pele**. She is regarded as the goddess of **fire** and **volcanoes**. According to the legends she lives in a volcanic crater on the big island. Many people in Hawaii still tell these stories today and treat the volcanoes with respect.

gewusst: Measured from the seabed, Mauna Kea is higher than Mount Everest.
On the summit of Mauna Kea stand large observatories, because the air there is very clear and dry.

teile.einleitung: The Yucatán Peninsula lies in Central America and belongs for the most part to Mexico. It is known for Maya cities, water-filled limestone holes and beaches on the Caribbean. Below it also lies a famous impact crater.
wichtigste: Yucatán lies between the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean Sea.
Most of it belongs to Mexico, and in the south Belize and Guatemala also have a share.
Mérida is the capital of the Mexican state of Yucatán.
The peninsula is made of limestone, so the water seeps away and flows underground.
Cenotes are water-filled limestone holes that were sacred to the Maya.
The Chicxulub crater is linked to the extinction of the dinosaurs.
Cancún is a well-known seaside resort on the Caribbean coast.

abschnitte.text: The **Yucatán Peninsula** juts out northwards in the south-east of Mexico. In the west and north lies the **Gulf of Mexico**, and in the east the **Caribbean Sea**. Most of it belongs to **Mexico**. In the south, **Belize** and the north of **Guatemala** also have a share of the peninsula. The land is flat and covered with forest and scrubland.

Yucatán is made of permeable **limestone**. A landscape like this is called **karst**. Rainwater seeps away quickly and flows in underground rivers and caves. That is why there are hardly any rivers on the surface. If the roof of a cave collapses, a hole full of water forms, a **cenote**. For the Maya, cenotes were important sources of water and sacred places.

On Yucatán lived the **Maya**, who built big cities such as Chichén Itzá. In the 16th century the Spanish came. In **1542** they founded the city of **Mérida** on the remains of an earlier Maya city. Today Mérida is the capital of the state of Yucatán. Many people on the peninsula still speak a Maya language as well.

On the north coast lies the **Chicxulub crater**, which today is hidden under rock. About **66 million years ago** an **asteroid** about 10 kilometres across struck there. The consequences for the climate of the whole Earth contributed to the **extinction of the dinosaurs**. It is thought that the ring of cenotes in the area is connected with the crater.

On the Caribbean coast lies **Cancún** in the state of Quintana Roo. It was built as a holiday area from **1970**. Today it is one of the most important tourist centres in Mexico. Many visitors also see Maya ruins and swim in cenotes.

gewusst: Under Yucatán lie some of the longest known underwater caves in the world.
The asteroid of Chicxulub was about as big as a whole mountain.

teile.einleitung: The Horn of Africa is a large peninsula in the east of Africa. It juts out into the Indian Ocean like a horn. Here there are hot deserts, deep depressions and important sea routes.
wichtigste: The Horn of Africa includes Somalia, Ethiopia, Eritrea and Djibouti.
Somalia has the longest coastline on the African mainland.
Ras Hafun in Somalia is the easternmost point of the African mainland.
Lake Assal in Djibouti is the lowest point in Africa.
The Danakil Depression is one of the hottest regions on Earth.
Droughts hit the people of the region hard again and again.

abschnitte.text: The Horn of Africa includes **Somalia**, **Ethiopia**, **Eritrea** and **Djibouti**. In the north lies the **Gulf of Aden** between Somalia and Yemen. The actual tip of the Horn is **Cape Guardafui** in northern Somalia. A little south of it lies **Ras Hafun**, the easternmost point of the African mainland. Somalia’s coast is over 3,000 kilometres long.

Between Djibouti and Yemen lies the strait of **Bab al-Mandab**. It is only about 30 kilometres wide and joins the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden. Many ships pass through here on their way to the **Suez Canal** and to Europe. That is why the region is very important for world trade.

In the north-east of Ethiopia lies the **Danakil Depression**. Part of it lies below sea level, and it is one of the hottest regions on Earth. There are salt flats and colourful hot springs there. In Djibouti, **Lake Assal** lies about 155 metres below sea level. It is the lowest point in Africa and extremely salty.

Many people live from **herding** goats, sheep and camels. When the rainy seasons fail, a **drought** follows. Then fields and pastures dry up, and famine threatens. Aid organisations, including some from Switzerland, support the people in such times.

**Asmara** is the capital of Eritrea. Eritrea used to be an Italian colony. In the 1930s many modern buildings went up there. Since 2017 Asmara has therefore been on the list of **UNESCO World Heritage Sites**.

gewusst: In Lake Assal the water is so salty that you float in it almost by yourself.
In Ethiopia some of the oldest fossils of early human ancestors have been found.

teile.einleitung: The hypocentre is the place inside the Earth where an earthquake begins. There the rock breaks, and earthquake waves spread out in all directions. Directly above it on the Earth’s surface lies the epicentre.
wichtigste: The hypocentre is also called the focus.
It is the point where the break in the rock begins.
The epicentre lies on the surface directly above the hypocentre.
From a focal depth of about 300 kilometres, people speak of a deep-focus earthquake.
The deepest known quakes lie at a depth of about 700 kilometres.
Shallow quakes of the same magnitude usually cause greater damage.

abschnitte.text: When layers of rock move against each other, stress builds up. At some point the rock breaks. The point where the break begins is the **hypocentre**, also called the **focus**. Directly above it on the Earth’s surface lies the **epicentre**. The distance between the two is the **focal depth**.

A distinction is made between **shallow**, **intermediate** and **deep** earthquakes. Quakes with a focus from about 300 kilometres down count as **deep-focus earthquakes**. The deepest quakes occur in sinking tectonic plates down to about **700 kilometres**. Deeper still, the rock is too plastic to break in a brittle way. In Switzerland the focus is usually only a few kilometres to about 30 kilometres deep.

In a shallow quake the waves travel only a **short way** to the surface. They are hardly weakened on the way, so the shaking is stronger. A deep quake of the same **magnitude**, by contrast, can be felt over a larger area, but is usually weaker. That is why shallow quakes often do more damage.

The **hypocentral distance** is the distance from a measuring station to the focus. The focal depth and the distance from the epicentre form the two shorter sides of a **right-angled triangle**. If the focus is 30 kilometres deep and the station is 40 kilometres from the epicentre, you calculate 30² plus 40², which gives 2,500. The square root of that is **50 kilometres**.

gewusst: The Swiss Seismological Service at ETH Zurich records hundreds of small quakes every year, and most of them nobody feels.
The word hypocentre comes from Greek: “hypo” means “under”.

teile.einleitung: Asia is the biggest continent on Earth, and its capitals are very varied. There are ancient imperial cities, cities high in the mountains and newly built capitals.
wichtigste: Beijing, in Chinese Běijīng, is the capital of China.
Seoul is the capital of South Korea, and Pyongyang is the capital of North Korea.
Tehran is the capital of Iran, and Baghdad is the capital of Iraq.
Ulaanbaatar in Mongolia is regarded as the coldest capital in the world.
Kathmandu is the capital of Nepal and lies in a valley in the Himalayas.
Naypyidaw has been the capital of Myanmar since 2005.
Astana has been the capital of Kazakhstan since 1997.

abschnitte.text: **Beijing**, in Chinese **Běijīng**, is the capital of the People’s Republic of China. There lies the **Forbidden City**, the former palace of the Chinese emperors. **Seoul** is the capital of **South Korea** and lies on the Han River in the north-west of the country. The capital of **North Korea**, by contrast, is **Pyongyang**.

**Tehran** is the capital of **Iran**. The city lies at the foot of the **Alborz Mountains** in the north of the country. From some parts of the city you can see snow-covered mountains. Do not mix it up: **Baghdad** is the capital of the neighbouring country of **Iraq**.

**Kathmandu**, the capital of **Nepal**, lies in a valley in the **Himalayas** at about 1400 metres. Many expeditions to **Mount Everest** start from Nepal. **Ulaanbaatar**, the capital of **Mongolia**, lies at about 1350 metres in the interior of the country. In winter the temperatures often fall below minus 30 degrees. It is therefore regarded as the **coldest capital in the world**.

Some countries have moved their capital. In **Myanmar** the government moved in **2005** from **Yangon** to the newly built city of **Naypyidaw**. Yangon, however, remained the biggest city. In **Kazakhstan**, **Astana** has been the capital since **1997** and replaced **Almaty**. From 2019 to 2022 Astana was called **Nur-Sultan**, and then the city got its old name back.

gewusst: The name Astana simply means “capital” in Kazakh.
Beijing means “northern capital”, while Tokyo means “eastern capital”.

teile.einleitung: Haiti is a country in the Caribbean. It lies in the west of the island of Hispaniola, which it shares with the Dominican Republic. Haiti has a special history: it came into being from a successful uprising of enslaved people.
wichtigste: Haiti lies in the west of the Caribbean island of Hispaniola.
The capital and biggest city is Port-au-Prince.
Haiti was a French colony and became independent in 1804.
Haiti was the first state to come into being from a successful slave uprising.
The official languages are French and Haitian Creole.
On 12 January 2010 a severe earthquake destroyed large parts of the capital.
The mountain fortress Citadelle Laferrière is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: Haiti lies on the island of **Hispaniola** in the Caribbean. Haiti makes up the west of the island, and the Dominican Republic the larger east. The country is very mountainous. The capital **Port-au-Prince** lies on a large bay in the west and is the biggest city in the country. Haiti is one of the poorest countries in the Americas.

In the 18th century Haiti was a rich **French colony** with big sugar plantations. Very many enslaved people from Africa had to work there. They rose up against colonial rule. Important leaders were **Toussaint Louverture** and **Jean-Jacques Dessalines**. In **1804** Haiti became independent. It was the first state to come into being from a successful slave uprising.

Haiti has two official languages: **French** and **Haitian Creole**. Haitian Creole is a **creole language** that developed mainly from French and contains many French words. Almost everyone in Haiti speaks Haitian Creole in everyday life. French is used mainly in schools, offices and newspapers.

After independence, Haiti feared that the French might return. That is why, at the start of the 19th century, the mighty **Citadelle Laferrière** was built on a mountain in the north. It is one of the biggest fortresses in the Americas. Today, together with palace ruins nearby, it is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

On **12 January 2010** a strong **earthquake** hit Haiti. It destroyed large parts of Port-au-Prince, including many houses, schools and government buildings. Very many people died or lost their homes. Many countries sent help, including **Switzerland**. The rebuilding took many years.

gewusst: After the USA, Haiti was the second country in the Americas to make itself independent of its colonial power.
The name Haiti comes from the language of the Taíno, the original inhabitants of the island, and means roughly “mountainous land”.

teile.einleitung: The Indian Plate is a tectonic plate on which India lies. About 50 million years ago it collided with Eurasia. This created the Himalayas, the highest mountain range on Earth, and the Tibetan Plateau.
wichtigste: India first broke away from Africa together with Madagascar and separated from Madagascar about 90 million years ago.
Before the collision India moved north at about 15 centimetres a year.
About 50 million years ago the collision with Eurasia began.
In the process the Tethys Ocean closed.
The summit of Mount Everest consists of marine limestone with fossils.
The crust under Tibet is about 70 kilometres thick.

abschnitte.text: India used to lie far in the south, close to Africa. Together with **Madagascar** it broke away from Africa. About **90 million years ago** it also separated from Madagascar. Then India moved north very fast, at about **15 centimetres a year**. This made it one of the fastest known plates.

On its way India travelled over a **hotspot**, a hot place in the Earth’s mantle. About **66 million years ago** huge amounts of lava poured out there. This is how the **basalt sheets** of the **Deccan Traps** came about. They cover large parts of western India. The hotspot lies today under the island of **Réunion**.

In front of India lay the **Tethys** Ocean. Its floor sank beneath Eurasia until the sea closed. About **50 million years ago** the **collision** began. Since then India has been pushing north and lifting up the **Himalayas** and **Tibet**. Today it moves only about 4 to 5 centimetres a year. That is why the summit of **Mount Everest** consists of **marine limestone** with fossils, which once lay on the sea floor.

In this collision two **continental plates** meet. Continental crust is too light to sink deep into the mantle. That is why hardly any magma forms, and there are hardly any active volcanoes in the High Himalayas. Instead the crust is piled up. Under Tibet it is about **70 kilometres** thick, roughly twice as thick as normal.

Because India keeps pushing north, there are **earthquakes** in the region again and again. On 25 April 2015 the **Gorkha earthquake**, with a magnitude of 7.8, shook **Nepal**. It occurred at the place where India is being pushed under the Himalayas. The Alps too, by the way, came about through a collision of plates, namely Africa and Europe.

gewusst: Even today the Himalayas grow a little higher every year.
On the summit of Mount Everest you can find fossils of sea creatures.

teile.einleitung: The Homestead Act was a law of the USA from 1862. It promised settlers a piece of land almost for free if they lived on it and farmed it. This is how the American West came to be heavily settled.
wichtigste: The Homestead Act was passed in 1862 under President Abraham Lincoln.
Settlers could receive 160 acres of land, which is about 65 hectares.
They had to live on the land and farm it for five years.
After that the land belonged to them, for a small fee.
The law encouraged above all the settlement of the Great Plains.
For the Indigenous peoples, the settlement meant the loss of land.

abschnitte.text: In 1862 President **Abraham Lincoln** signed the Homestead Act. A **homestead** is a farm with land on which a family lives. The law came into force on 1 January 1863. The government wanted many people to settle in the wide West and to farm there.

Anyone who applied received **160 acres** of land, about 65 hectares. In return they had to build a house, lay out fields and live on the land for five years. Only then did they become the real **owner**. Unmarried women and, later, freed slaves could also apply for land. For its time this was progressive.

Many settlers moved to the **Great Plains**, a huge grassland in the middle of the USA. There were hardly any trees there, so some built their houses from sods of turf. Drought, storms and hard winters made life difficult. Not everyone lasted the five years, and some gave up their farms again.

The land that was handed out was often the home of **Indigenous peoples**. With the settlers, these peoples lost their hunting grounds and were pushed into reservations. That is why the Homestead Act is seen today with mixed feelings. It gave many families a chance, but took the land away from others.

gewusst: Through the law, in total about a tenth of the area of the USA was handed over to private owners.
The Homestead Act lasted a very long time: it was only repealed in 1976, and in Alaska a little later still.

teile.einleitung: Hudson Bay is a huge inland sea in the north of Canada. It is about 30 times as big as Switzerland. In winter it mostly freezes over, and many polar bears live on its shores.
wichtigste: Hudson Bay is a large, shallow inland sea with salt water.
It is named after the English navigator Henry Hudson.
It is joined to the Atlantic by the Hudson Strait.
In winter it is almost completely covered with ice.
The town of Churchill is known as the “polar bear capital of the world”.
Its southern arm is called James Bay.

abschnitte.text: Hudson Bay is an **inland sea** with salt water. It is very big, but rather shallow. Through the **Hudson Strait** between Baffin Island and Quebec it is joined to the **Atlantic**, and in the north also to the Arctic Ocean. In the south lies **James Bay** between Ontario and Quebec. Many rivers flow into it, and they are used for hydroelectric power stations.

The English navigator **Henry Hudson** explored the bay in 1610. He was looking for a sea route to Asia. The following year his crew mutinied and set him adrift in a small boat. Hudson was never seen again. The bay still bears his name today.

In 1670 the **Hudson’s Bay Company** was founded. It received the right from the English king to trade throughout the whole region around the bay. The traders exchanged mainly **beaver pelts** with Indigenous peoples for goods such as knives, kettles and cloth. The company is one of the oldest trading businesses in the world.

In winter Hudson Bay mostly **freezes** over. In summer the ice melts, and ships can sail only a few months of the year. In **Churchill** in Manitoba, many **polar bears** wait on the shore in autumn. As soon as the sea freezes, they go out onto the ice and hunt seals. That is why Churchill is called the “polar bear capital of the world”.

gewusst: In summer thousands of beluga whales come into the river mouths on Hudson Bay.
Hudson Bay is so big that several Canadian provinces and territories lie on it.

teile.einleitung: High fog is a grey blanket of cloud that in winter often lies for days over the Swiss Central Plateau. Below it is dull and cold, while in the mountains above the fog the Sun shines.
wichtigste: High fog is a low, grey layer of cloud over the lowlands.
It forms mainly in autumn and winter in high-pressure weather.
Cold air collects below and warmer air lies above it: this is called an inversion.
Above the high fog it is often sunny, and you can see a sea of fog.
The Swiss Central Plateau between the Jura and the Alps is especially often affected.

abschnitte.text: In **high-pressure weather** in autumn and winter, the air near the ground cools strongly on clear nights. The cold, heavy air collects in the lowlands. Above it lies **warmer air**. This upside-down layering is called an **inversion**. The moisture in the cold air forms a **layer of cloud** at the boundary. Because the winter Sun is weak, this layer often does not dissolve for days.

The **Swiss Central Plateau** lies like a trough between the **Jura** and the **Alps**. The cold air cannot flow away well there. That is why high fog lies especially often over the Central Plateau. Sometimes it stays grey like this for weeks. Often a weak **bise** blows as well, which makes it feel even colder.

If you climb or ride up a mountain, you can leave the fog behind. Up there the **Sun** often shines, and the sky is blue. From there you can see the **sea of fog**: the blanket of cloud lies like a white lake below you, and only the peaks stick out. On grey days many people therefore escape to viewpoints such as the Rigi, Pilatus or heights in the Jura.

gewusst: On days of high fog it can be clearly warmer on a mountain than below on the Central Plateau.

teile.einleitung: The Humboldt Current is a cold ocean current in the Pacific off the west coast of South America. It flows from south to north along Chile and Peru. It shapes the climate on the coast and is one of the richest fishing areas on Earth.
wichtigste: The Humboldt Current is named after Alexander von Humboldt and is also called the Peru Current.
It flows along the coast of South America from south to north.
Cold water from the south and rising deep water make it cool.
It contributes to the extreme dryness of the Atacama.
The nutrient-rich water feeds huge shoals of anchoveta.
Branches of the current cool the sea around the Galápagos Islands.

abschnitte.text: The naturalist **Alexander von Humboldt** measured the water temperature off the coast of Peru around 1802 on his journey through the Americas. He found that the water was surprisingly cold. The current was later named after him. It is also called the **Peru Current**.

The Humboldt Current brings water from the cold regions in the south towards the north. In addition, cold **deep water** rises off the coast, which is called **upwelling**. That is why the water temperatures off Lima are often clearly below 20 °C, although the city lies in the tropics. Off Ecuador the current turns west.

The cold water cools the lowest layer of air. Warmer air lies above it, so hardly any rain clouds rise. This is how the **Atacama** comes about on the coast, one of the driest deserts on Earth. In winter a fine fog with drizzle, the **garúa**, often lies over Lima. On some slopes plants live only on this fog. These green islands are called **lomas**.

The rising deep water is rich in nutrients. Huge shoals of the **anchoveta**, the Peruvian anchovy, live on them. It is processed mainly into fishmeal and fish oil. Many seabirds feed on the fish. Their droppings, **guano**, were mined in the 19th century as a valuable fertiliser.

Branches of the Humboldt Current keep the sea around the **Galápagos Islands** cool and rich in nutrients. That is why the **Galápagos penguin** can live there. It is the only species of penguin that also occurs north of the equator. In an **El Niño** the water becomes warmer, and fish and seabirds find less food.

gewusst: In the Atacama there are places where no measurable rain falls for years.
Off Peru, in some years, more fish are caught than almost anywhere else in the world.

teile.einleitung: Japan consists of a long chain of islands in the western Pacific, the **Japanese Archipelago**. An archipelago is a group of islands. Four large main islands form the core, and thousands of smaller islands are added to them.
wichtigste: The four main islands are Hokkaidō, Honshū, Shikoku and Kyūshū.
**Honshū** is the biggest main island.
**Hokkaidō** lies furthest to the north.
**Shikoku** is the smallest of the four main islands.
The **Seikan Tunnel** joins Honshū and Hokkaidō under the sea.
Okinawa belongs to the **Ryūkyū Islands** in the south.

abschnitte.text: From north to south they are **Hokkaidō**, **Honshū**, **Shikoku** and **Kyūshū**. Honshū is the biggest and most important island, and Tokyo, Osaka and Kyoto lie there. Hokkaidō in the north has long, snowy winters. Shikoku is the smallest main island. Kyūshū lies furthest to the south-west and is close to Korea.

Besides the main islands, over 14,000 smaller islands belong to Japan. In the south the long chain of the **Ryūkyū Islands** stretches almost to Taiwan. The best known is **Okinawa**. There it is warm all year round, and there are coral reefs. In the north, by contrast, it is cool, and on Hokkaidō there is a lot of snow in winter.

The main islands are joined by bridges and tunnels. The **Seikan Tunnel** runs under a strait from Honshū to Hokkaidō. It is over 50 kilometres long and was opened in 1988. There are tunnels to Kyūshū too, and large bridges lead to Shikoku.

The archipelago lies on the **Pacific Ring of Fire**, where several plates of the Earth’s crust meet. That is why in Japan there are many **volcanoes** and frequent **earthquakes**. Mountains cover a large part of the country, and most people live on the plains along the coasts.

gewusst: The Seikan Tunnel is among the longest railway tunnels in the world, about as long as the Gotthard Base Tunnel.
From Hokkaidō to the southernmost islands, Japan stretches over about 3,000 kilometres.

teile.einleitung: A hurricane is a very strong tropical storm that forms over warm sea. It brings violent wind, a great deal of rain and often floods. Hurricanes occur mainly in the Atlantic and the Caribbean.
wichtigste: A hurricane is a strong tropical cyclone with violent wind and a lot of rain.
It forms over sea water of at least about 26 °C.
In the calm centre, the eye, it is almost windless.
Hurricanes are divided into five categories, and category 5 is the strongest.
Every hurricane is given a name from a fixed list.
In the western Pacific near Asia, such storms are called typhoons.
On the coast, hurricanes often bring a storm surge.

abschnitte.text: A hurricane needs **very warm sea water** of at least about 26 °C. The water evaporates, the moist air rises and forms huge thunderclouds. In the process a lot of energy is released, which drives the storm. Because the Earth turns, the air starts to spin. Over land a hurricane loses its strength, because the warm water is missing.

A hurricane is like a huge whirl. In its centre lies the **eye**. There it is almost windless and often even clear. Around the eye lies the **eyewall**. Here the strongest winds and the heaviest rain rage. When the eye passes over a place, it briefly seems as if the storm is over.

Hurricanes are divided into **categories 1 to 5** on the **Saffir-Simpson scale**. Category 5 is the strongest. Every storm is given a **first name** from a fixed list. This makes it easier to tell several storms apart. In the western Pacific near Asia such storms are called **typhoons**, and in the Indian Ocean **cyclones**.

The strong wind can strip roofs and knock over trees. Especially dangerous is the **storm surge**: the wind pushes the sea water against the coast, and the water rises high. Together with the heavy rain, **floods** often follow. That is why people on the coast are warned in good time and sometimes taken to safety.

Researchers watch hurricanes with **satellites** in space. In the pictures you can see the great whirls of cloud and work out where the storm is heading. Special aeroplanes even fly into the middle of the storm to take measurements. In this way weather services can warn early.

gewusst: A large hurricane can be several hundred kilometres across.
In Switzerland there are no hurricanes, because the warm sea they need is missing.

teile.einleitung: Contour lines are lines on a map that join points of the same height. With them you can recognise mountains, valleys and steep slopes on a flat sheet of paper. On every Swiss national map you will find many contour lines.
wichtigste: A contour line joins all points of the same height above sea level.
If contour lines lie close together, the terrain is steep.
The difference in height between two lines is called the contour interval.
On the 1:25,000 national map the contour interval is 10 metres.
Thicker, labelled lines are called index contours.
Swiss height figures refer to the Repère Pierre du Niton in Geneva.

abschnitte.text: Imagine you cut a mountain horizontally into slices of equal thickness. The edges of the slices are the **contour lines**. Each line runs through points that lie at the same height above sea level. If the lines lie **close** together, the terrain is **steep**. If they lie far apart, it is flat.

The difference in height between two neighbouring lines is called the **contour interval**. On the **1:25,000 national map** from **swisstopo** it is 10 metres, and on the 1:50,000 map it is 20 metres. Every fifth or tenth line is drawn thicker and often labelled with its height. These lines are called **index contours** and make reading the map easier.

Several closed rings that get higher towards the inside show a **hill** or **peak**. In a stream valley the contour lines form a **V**. The point of the V points **uphill**, because the stream has cut into the terrain. With a ridge it is the other way round: there the point faces downhill.

For all heights in Switzerland to fit together, a common starting point is needed. This is the **Repère Pierre du Niton**, a boulder in **Lake Geneva**. Its height of 373.6 metres is the basis for Swiss height figures. From there, heights were surveyed across the whole country.

gewusst: Swiss national maps are known worldwide for their beautiful and precise depiction of the mountains.
Next to the Pierre du Niton lies a second boulder, the Pierre de Dyolat.

teile.einleitung: Gondwana was a huge ancient continent in the Southern Hemisphere of the Earth. Through the slow drifting of the continents it broke up into today’s South America, Africa, Antarctica, Australia and India.
wichtigste: About 550 million years ago, Gondwana was completely joined together.
Gondwana included South America, Africa, Antarctica, Australia and India, but not North America.
The name comes from a region in India.
The fossil plant Glossopteris is found on all the Gondwana continents.
When it broke up, the South Atlantic formed between Africa and South America.
Coal in Antarctica shows that forests once grew there.

abschnitte.text: The continents of the Earth move, but only a few centimetres a year. About **550 million years ago**, several landmasses in the south were joined into a single continent: **Gondwana**. It included today’s **South America**, **Africa**, **Antarctica**, **Australia**, **India** and Madagascar. **North America** was **not** part of it, but belonged to a northern continent. Later Gondwana joined with the northern continents to form the supercontinent **Pangaea**.

The name comes from a **region in India**, the land of the Gond people. There, geologists in the 19th century found special layers of rock. Similar layers were later discovered in Africa, South America and Australia too. The Austrian geologist Eduard Suess gave the old continent the name Gondwana. Alfred Wegener used such finds for his theory of **continental drift**.

An important piece of evidence is the fossil plant **Glossopteris**. Its remains are found on **all the Gondwana continents**, including Antarctica. Its seeds could hardly have been carried across a sea, so the lands must have been joined. In 1969 the reptile **Lystrosaurus** from the Triassic, already known from Africa and India, was also found in Antarctica. This strongly supported the Gondwana theory.

Gondwana went through a great ice age in the **Carboniferous and Permian periods**. **Glacier deposits** in countries that are warm today, such as India, Africa and Brazil, bear witness to this. Conversely, in **Antarctica**, which is icy today, there are deposits of **coal**. Coal forms from plants, so **forests** once grew there. Antarctica used to lie in a different place and had a different climate.

About 180 million years ago Gondwana began to break apart. Between Africa and **South America** the **South Atlantic** slowly opened up. India broke away and moved north until it collided with Asia, and the Himalayas were folded up as a result. When Antarctica had separated completely from Australia and South America, an **ocean current** could circle the continent. It kept warm water away and so helped the **glaciation** of Antarctica.

gewusst: The coastlines of South America and Africa fit together almost like puzzle pieces because they were once joined.
The current around Antarctica is now the strongest ocean current on Earth.

teile.einleitung: Groundwater is water that fills the hollow spaces in the soil and rock underground. It forms mainly from rain that seeps into the ground. In Switzerland, groundwater is the most important source of drinking water.
wichtigste: Rainwater that soaks into the ground is called infiltration.
A layer that can store and carry groundwater is called an aquifer.
About 80 per cent of the drinking water in Switzerland comes from groundwater and springs.
In limestone rock, for example in the Jura, there are karst aquifers.
Nitrate from intensive farming can pollute groundwater.
Fossil groundwater is very old and hardly renews itself.

abschnitte.text: Part of the rain runs off or evaporates. Another part soaks into the ground. This is called **infiltration**. The water seeps down through soil, sand and gravel. There it fills pores and cracks in the rock. A layer that can store and carry a lot of water is called an **aquifer**. A dense layer such as clay, on the other hand, lets hardly any water through, and is called an **aquiclude**.

According to the Federal Office for the Environment, about **80 per cent** of the drinking water in Switzerland comes from groundwater and springs. The rest comes mainly from lakes. The layers of gravel and sand in the valleys of big rivers are particularly productive. In **bank filtration**, wells stand close to a river. The river water seeps through gravel and sand to the wells and is cleaned on the way. In the **Jura** there are **karst aquifers**. There the water has dissolved caves and cracks in the limestone and flows quickly, almost without being filtered.

If an aquifer lies under a dense layer and its water comes from higher-lying areas, it is under pressure. This is called **confined groundwater**. If you drill into it, the water rises by itself up above the surface. This is an **artesian well**. How groundwater flows through sand and rock is described by **Darcy’s law** of 1856. The French engineer Henry Darcy had studied in Dijon how water flows through sand filters.

Fertiliser and liquid manure contain nitrogen. It can get into groundwater as **nitrate**. That is why **intensive farming** is a main source of it. Pesticides can also pollute the water. Another problem is **overuse**. Under the Great Plains of the USA the **Ogallala Aquifer** is used so heavily for irrigation that the water levels are falling.

Some groundwater is very old. It formed thousands of years ago, when the climate was damper, for example under today’s **Sahara**. It is called **fossil groundwater**. Because it hardly rains there now, it almost does not renew itself. Anyone who uses it is using up a store that will not come back.

gewusst: Groundwater can stay in the ground for years or even thousands of years before it comes back to the surface.
Under the Sahara lie huge stores of ancient groundwater.

teile.einleitung: “Hoy No Circula” is a programme in Mexico City against air pollution. In Spanish the name means “Today it does not drive”. Depending on the number plate, cars are not allowed to drive on certain days.
wichtigste: The programme has existed in Mexico City since 1989.
Depending on the last digit of the number plate, cars are not allowed to drive on certain days.
The aim is to reduce air pollution.
Mexico City lies in a high valley in which dirty air easily gets trapped.
Air quality has improved since then.

abschnitte.text: Mexico City is one of the biggest cities in the world. It lies at over 2,000 metres in a **high valley** surrounded by mountains. The exhaust fumes of millions of cars and many factories cannot escape easily. Especially in calm weather, **smog** forms, a haze of dirty air hanging over the city.

Since **1989** the programme **“Hoy No Circula”** has applied in Mexico City. Every car has one day a week on which it is not allowed to drive. Which day that is depends on the **last digit of the number plate**. Newer and cleaner cars often get an exemption. In this way the roads are relieved and fewer exhaust fumes are given off.

Since it was introduced, **air quality** in Mexico City has improved. Cleaner engines and better petrol have also helped. Critics say that some families bought a second, often older car to get round the ban. Other cities around the world have also tried similar driving bans.

gewusst: When the air is especially bad, Mexico City can impose extra driving bans on even more cars.

teile.einleitung: The Great Migration is one of the biggest animal migrations in the world. Every year well over a million wildebeest travel across the savannahs of East Africa. They follow the rain and the fresh grass.
wichtigste: The migration leads through the Serengeti in Tanzania and the Masai Mara in Kenya.
Mainly wildebeest take part, along with zebras and gazelles.
There are well over a million wildebeest.
The animals look for fresh grass, which grows after the rain.
The herds travel in a big circle every year.
Crocodiles lie in wait when they cross the Mara.

abschnitte.titel: Millions of wildebeest on the move
abschnitte.text: In the Great Migration, huge herds of **wildebeest** travel across the savannah. There are **well over a million** animals. With them travel **zebras** and gazelles as well. The zebras like to eat the tall grass, and the wildebeest the shorter grass underneath. This way the animals hardly get in each other’s way.

The wildebeest migrate because they are looking for **fresh grass**. Where it has rained, new grass grows. Every year the herds travel in a big **circle** between the **Serengeti** in Tanzania and the **Masai Mara** in Kenya. When a year is over, the journey begins again from the start. Where the herds are and when depends on the rain and is a little different every year.

On the way the wildebeest have to cross the **Mara**, a river in Kenya and Tanzania. This is very dangerous. The banks are steep, and the current can be strong. In the water, large **Nile crocodiles** lie in wait. On land, lions and hyenas are waiting. Even so, the great majority of animals make it to the other bank.

Almost all **wildebeest calves** are born within **a few weeks**. This happens in the rainy season in the south of the Serengeti, where there is then a lot of grass. Because so many calves are there at the same time, they are better protected together. A calf can stand up just **a few minutes** after birth. Soon after, it runs along with the herd.

gewusst: A newborn wildebeest calf can often stand after just a few minutes and soon afterwards run.
The Serengeti is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

teile.einleitung: The Great Dividing Range is the largest mountain range in Australia. It runs along the east coast from Queensland to Victoria. Although it is very long, its mountains are rather low.
wichtigste: The Great Dividing Range runs along the east coast of Australia.
It is about 3500 kilometres long.
The highest mountain is Mount Kosciuszko at 2228 metres.
The mountain range is very old and heavily worn down.
It separates short coastal rivers in the east from the Murray-Darling system in the west.
On the eastern side it rains a lot, while the west is drier.

abschnitte.text: The Great Dividing Range is about **3500 kilometres** long and so the longest mountain range in Australia. The highest mountain is **Mount Kosciuszko** at 2228 metres. It is lower than the Säntis at 2502 metres. The range is **very old** and has been worn away over an unimaginably long time. Australia lies in the middle of a tectonic plate, far from zones where plates collide. That is why no new high mountains are growing here.

Damp air from the **Pacific** rises up the eastern slopes and falls as rain. West of the mountains it is therefore much drier. The range is also a **watershed**. On the eastern side, short, steep rivers flow straight into the sea. To the west, long rivers such as the Darling flow into the great **Murray-Darling Basin**.

West of Sydney lie the **Blue Mountains**. From a distance they shimmer bluish. This comes from fine **oil droplets** that eucalyptus trees give off into the air and that scatter the light. The steep sandstone gorges blocked the settlers’ way into the interior for a long time. It was only in 1813 that **Blaxland, Lawson and Wentworth** found a way across, by following the ridge instead of the valleys.

In the south of New South Wales lie the **Snowy Mountains**. In the Australian winter, roughly from June to September, you can ski there. From 1949 to 1974 the **Snowy Mountains Scheme** was built here. It channels water through tunnels to the western side of the range. There it is used for irrigation and drives hydroelectric power stations.

gewusst: The highest mountain in Australia is lower than many peaks in the Swiss Pre-Alps.
The blue colour of the Blue Mountains comes from eucalyptus oil in the air.

teile.einleitung: A houseboat is a boat that people live on. It has a kitchen, bed and living space like a small flat, only on the water. Houseboats exist in many countries, on canals, rivers and lakes.
wichtigste: On a houseboat you live as in a flat, but on the water.
In Amsterdam over 2000 houseboats lie on the canals.
The canals in Amsterdam are called grachten.
In Paris many houseboats lie on the Seine.
In England long, narrow boats travel on a big network of canals.
In Kerala in India, tourists stay overnight on houseboats made of wood and bamboo.
A houseboat is tied to the bank with strong ropes.

abschnitte.text: A **houseboat** is a floating home. It has a kitchen, a bed, a living space and often a small bathroom too. Some houseboats can sail, while others always lie in the same place. To stop it drifting away, a houseboat is tied to the bank with strong **ropes**. Electricity and water often come through pipes and cables from the bank.

Especially well known are the houseboats in **Amsterdam** in the Netherlands. The city has many canals, which are called **grachten**. On their banks lie over **2000 houseboats**. Some are converted old cargo ships, while others look like small houses on a floating box. A houseboat there is a proper home address.

In **England** there is a big network of **canals** that were once built for transporting goods. On them travel long, narrow boats, the so-called narrowboats. Many people live on them or take holidays on them. In **Paris** many boats lie on the banks of the **Seine**, which flows through the middle of the city. There too, people live on their boats.

In the south of **India** lies the state of **Kerala**. There is a maze of rivers, lakes and canals. In the past, boats carried rice and other goods there. Today many of them are used as **houseboats** for tourists. They are built of **wood** and **bamboo**, and you can stay overnight on them and travel slowly through the waterways.

gewusst: Some houseboats in Amsterdam are now museums or even a home for cats.
You can also take a holiday on a houseboat on some Swiss lakes and rivers.

teile.einleitung: In Europe there are about 45 states, and each has a capital. Some are huge metropolises such as Paris or London, others are small towns such as Vaduz in Liechtenstein. If you know the capitals, it is much easier to find your way around the map of Europe.
wichtigste: The capital of Portugal is Lisbon.
The capital of Poland is Warsaw.
The capital of Croatia is Zagreb.
Switzerland officially has no capital, and Bern is called the federal city.
The capitals of Switzerland’s neighbouring countries are Berlin, Paris, Rome, Vienna and Vaduz.
Brussels is the capital of Belgium and the seat of important institutions of the European Union.
The smallest capital in Europe is Vatican City, which is itself a state.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland officially has no capital, and **Bern** is called the **federal city**. Around Switzerland lie the capitals **Berlin** in Germany, **Paris** in France, **Rome** in Italy, **Vienna** in Austria and **Vaduz** in Liechtenstein. With a few thousand inhabitants, Vaduz is one of the smallest capitals in Europe. By train you can reach Paris, Milan or Vienna from Zurich or Basel in a few hours.

The capital of Portugal is **Lisbon**, which lies on the Atlantic at the mouth of the River Tagus. Spain’s capital Madrid, by contrast, lies in the middle of the country on a plateau. **London** is the capital of the United Kingdom and one of the biggest cities in Europe. **Brussels** is the capital of Belgium, and many institutions of the European Union have their seat there.

The capital of Poland is **Warsaw** on the Vistula. It was almost completely destroyed in the Second World War and then rebuilt, and its old town is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Prague is the capital of the Czech Republic and Budapest the capital of Hungary. The biggest city in Europe is **Moscow**, the capital of Russia.

The capital of Croatia is **Zagreb**, not the well-known coastal cities of Split or Dubrovnik. Athens in Greece is one of the oldest cities in Europe and famous for the Acropolis. **Rome** is the capital of Italy, and in the middle of Rome lies Vatican City, the smallest state in the world. Other capitals in the south-east are Belgrade in Serbia and Sofia in Bulgaria.

In the north lie Copenhagen in Denmark, Oslo in Norway, Stockholm in Sweden and Helsinki in Finland. **Reykjavík** in Iceland is the northernmost capital of an independent state in the world. Many Nordic capitals lie right on the sea and have big ports. Stockholm is built on many islands.

You can learn capitals well with a **map of Europe** and memory aids. Often it helps to practise Switzerland’s neighbouring countries first and then work on region by region. Be careful with countries whose biggest city is not the capital. Travel, football matches or the news also help you to remember the names.

begriffe.erklaerung: The city in which the government and parliament of a country have their seat.
The official name for Bern.
A very big and important city.
An association of many European states that work closely together.

gewusst: Rome is the only capital within whose city area another state lies, Vatican City.
Bratislava and Vienna are only about 60 kilometres apart and are the two capitals in Europe that lie closest together.

teile.einleitung: The **Isthmus of Panama** is a narrow strip of land that joins North America and South America. The country of **Panama** lies on it. Right through the middle runs the famous **Panama Canal**, which joins the Atlantic with the Pacific.
wichtigste: An isthmus is a **land bridge** between two large landmasses.
Panama borders Costa Rica in the west and Colombia in the east.
The capital city is **Panama City**.
The Panama Canal saves ships the long journey around South America.
Since 1999 Panama has run the canal itself.
When North and South America grew together, animals could walk across.

abschnitte.text: An **isthmus** is a narrow strip of land between two seas that joins two larger landmasses. The Isthmus of Panama joins **North America** and **South America**. On the map Panama looks like a narrow, curved strip. It belongs to **Central America**, the narrow part of the Americas between Mexico and South America. In the west lies Costa Rica, and in the east Colombia.

Right across Panama people built a **canal for ships**, which opened in 1914. Before that, ships had to sail all the way around the southern tip of South America. Through the canal the route becomes much shorter. **Locks** raise the ships and lower them again, because the canal runs over a lake in the interior of the country. It was built by the USA, and since 1999 **Panama** itself has run it.

A few million years ago North and South America were separated by sea. Then the isthmus rose out of the sea. Now animals could walk **on foot** from north to south and the other way round. In this way cats and deer, for example, came to South America and armadillos went north. In the rainforest of Panama today **sloths** hang slowly in the trees.

The capital city, **Panama City**, lies on the Pacific, close to the entrance of the canal. It has many skyscrapers and an old town from the Spanish colonial period. The canal is very important for the country, because the fees paid by ships bring in a lot of money.

gewusst: A ship usually needs about 8 to 10 hours to pass through the Panama Canal.
Because the isthmus winds from west to east, in some places in Panama the Sun rises over the Pacific.

teile.einleitung: High above our heads blows a narrow band of very strong wind: the **jet stream**. It flows at a height of about 8 to 12 kilometres, mostly from west to east around the Earth. It is very important for the weather and for aeroplanes.
wichtigste: The jet stream blows at a height of about 8 to 12 kilometres.
The wind there can reach up to about 400 km/h.
In each hemisphere there are mainly the **polar front jet** and the **subtropical jet**.
The polar front jet arises from large differences in temperature between air masses.
In the Northern Hemisphere it is usually strongest in winter.
Flights to the east are often faster thanks to a tailwind.

abschnitte.text: A **jet stream** is like a river of air at great height. It is several hundred kilometres wide, but only a few kilometres thick. In its centre the wind reaches very high speeds, sometimes **up to about 400 km/h**. It usually blows from west to east. The Japanese meteorologist **Wasaburo Oishi** discovered it in the 1920s using pilot balloons.

The **polar front jet** forms where cold air from the north and warm air from the south meet. The greater the **difference in temperature**, the stronger the wind. In winter this difference is greatest in the Northern Hemisphere, so the jet is then usually at its strongest. Further south blows the **subtropical jet**.

The jet stream does not run straight, but winds in great waves around the Earth. These waves are called **Rossby waves**. They steer low-pressure areas with rain and high-pressure areas with fine weather. If the jet lies over Europe, it often brings changeable weather to Switzerland. If the waves stay in place for a long time, it can stay hot or wet for weeks.

Aeroplanes fly at about the height of the jet stream. A flight from **Zurich to New York** therefore usually takes longer than the return flight, because on the outward flight there is a **headwind**. On the return flight the tailwind pushes. In the Second World War Japan used the jet stream to send **balloon bombs** across the Pacific to North America.

gewusst: A flight from New York to Europe can sometimes be over an hour shorter thanks to the jet stream than in the opposite direction.
In German the jet stream is called “Strahlstrom”, which means roughly “jet current”.

teile.einleitung: In **just-in-time production**, parts are delivered exactly when they are needed in the factory. This means hardly any large stores are needed. The method comes from the Japanese car maker **Toyota** and is used today in many industries.
wichtigste: The aim is to deliver parts exactly when they are needed.
Just in time was developed at **Toyota**, above all by **Taiichi Ohno**.
Resupply is requested with **kanban** cards.
The system works on the **pull principle**.
With **just in sequence**, the parts even arrive in the exact order of assembly.
Interruptions to deliveries can quickly stop production.

abschnitte.text: In the past, factories had large **stores** with many parts kept in reserve. That costs space and money. With **just in time**, the parts arrive only shortly before they are fitted. The Japanese car maker **Toyota** developed this idea as part of its production system. The engineer **Taiichi Ohno** is regarded as the main developer.

With just in time, consumption decides what is delivered. This is called the **pull principle**, from the English word “pull”. When a container of parts becomes empty, a card goes back to the place that makes or supplies the parts. This card is called a **kanban**, Japanese for “card” or “signboard”. In this way only what is really needed is made again.

Because the factory hardly stores any parts any more, many **lorries** are on the road delivering the parts on time. It is therefore said that the store is now **on the road**. Many suppliers therefore settle close to the assembly plant. With **just in sequence**, the parts even arrive in exactly the order in which the cars are built on the line, for example seats in the right colour.

Just in time saves money, but it is vulnerable. If one delivery fails, the whole of production soon stands still. This was shown in March 2021, when the big container ship **“Ever Given”** got stuck in the **Suez Canal** and blocked this important trade route for days. During the coronavirus pandemic, too, many factories lacked important parts. Since then some firms have again been keeping somewhat larger stocks.

gewusst: Among other things, Taiichi Ohno drew inspiration from American supermarkets, where shelves are refilled only when goods have been taken away.
Swiss retailers also work with precisely planned deliveries, so that fresh goods do not have to be stored for long.

teile.einleitung: The Great Lakes are five huge, connected lakes in North America. They lie between the USA and Canada. Together they form the largest area of fresh water on Earth.
wichtigste: The five Great Lakes are Lake Superior, Lake Michigan, Lake Huron, Lake Erie and Lake Ontario.
They lie between the USA and Canada.
Lake Superior is the biggest of the five.
Only Lake Michigan lies entirely in the USA.
Niagara Falls lies between Lake Erie and Lake Ontario.
The St Lawrence River carries the water into the Atlantic.
The lakes hold about a fifth of the fresh water in lakes and rivers on Earth.

abschnitte.text: The five Great Lakes are called **Lake Superior**, **Lake Michigan**, **Lake Huron**, **Lake Erie** and **Lake Ontario**. They are connected by rivers and straits. The border between the **USA** and **Canada** runs through four of them. Only **Lake Michigan** lies completely in the USA. The lakes formed at the end of the Ice Age, when huge glaciers had gouged out deep basins and then melted.

**Lake Superior** is the biggest of the five. It is so big that you cannot see the other shore. On the lakes there are waves, storms and even large cargo ships. Together the Great Lakes hold about **a fifth** of the fresh water in lakes and rivers on Earth. Only Lake Baikal in Russia has a similar amount of water.

abschnitte.titel: Niagara Falls and the St Lawrence River
abschnitte.text: The water flows on from lake to lake. The Niagara River connects Lake Erie with Lake Ontario. On the way it plunges over the famous **Niagara Falls**. From Lake Ontario the water flows into the **St Lawrence River**. This flows into the **Atlantic Ocean**. Through canals and locks, ships can travel from the sea deep into the interior of the continent.

Many big cities lie on the Great Lakes. **Chicago** lies on the south-western shore of Lake Michigan and is one of the biggest cities in the USA. **Toronto**, the biggest city in Canada, lies on the northern shore of Lake Ontario. Detroit, Cleveland and Buffalo are also near the lakes. The lakes supply drinking water for millions of people.

gewusst: Cargo ships longer than 300 metres sail on the Great Lakes.
You can remember the five lakes with the English word “HOMES”: Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie, Superior.

teile.einleitung: In the tropical Andes it is hot at the foot of the mountains and icy on the peaks. In between lie different altitudinal zones, each with its own climate. People grow different plants in each zone.
wichtigste: The altitudinal zones are called Tierra caliente, Tierra templada, Tierra fría and Tierra helada.
In the hot Tierra caliente, bananas, cocoa and sugar cane grow.
In the Tierra templada mainly coffee is grown.
In the cool Tierra fría, potatoes and cereals thrive.
The Tierra helada serves as pasture for llamas and alpacas.
Alexander von Humboldt described the altitudinal zones in detail for the first time around 1800.

abschnitte.text: The lowest zone is called **Tierra caliente**, which means “hot land” in Spanish. It stretches from sea level to about 800 to 1,000 metres. Here it is warm all year round. Tropical plants such as **bananas**, **cocoa** and **sugar cane** are grown.

Above it lies the **Tierra templada**, the “temperate land”. It stretches from about 1,000 to 2,000 or 2,500 metres. Here it is neither too hot nor frosty. That is why **coffee** thrives especially well here. Many big cities of the Andes lie in this pleasant zone.

The **Tierra fría**, the “cold land”, lies roughly between 2,500 and 3,500 to 4,000 metres. **Potatoes** and cereals are typical. The potato originally comes from the Andes. **Quinoa** is also grown on the highlands up to about 4,000 metres. Botanically it is not a true cereal, and it was already a staple food for the Incas.

At the very top lies the **Tierra helada**, the “icy land”. Farming is hardly possible here any more. The grasslands serve as pasture for **llamas** and **alpacas**. In the north, in Ecuador and Colombia, the grassland is damp and misty, and is called **páramo**. In Peru and Bolivia it is drier and is called **puna**.

For every 100 metres of height it gets about **0.5 to 0.6 °C** cooler. That explains the different zones. The naturalist **Alexander von Humboldt** climbed the volcano **Chimborazo** in Ecuador to a great height in 1802. In his famous “Naturgemälde of the Andes”, a painting-like diagram of nature, he recorded which plants grow at which height.

gewusst: In the Andes there are thousands of different varieties of potato.
In the páramo, rosette plants such as the espeletia grow, which look like small palm trees.

teile.einleitung: The Earth’s crust rests on the viscous mantle, in a similar way to icebergs floating in water. This balance is called **isostasy**. It explains why mountains have deep roots and why some countries are still rising today.
wichtigste: Isostasy is the floating balance of the Earth’s crust on the mantle.
The term was coined by the US geologist **Clarence Dutton** in 1889.
According to **Airy**, high mountains have deep roots.
According to **Pratt**, higher blocks of crust have a lower density.
Scandinavia is rising because the load of the Ice Age ice has gone.
Parts of the Swiss Alps are rising today by about 1 millimetre a year.

abschnitte.text: Only a small part of an iceberg sticks out of the water, and the greatest part lies below. It is similar with the **Earth’s crust**. It is lighter than the **mantle** beneath it and floats on it, so to speak. The mantle is solid, but over very long periods of time it behaves like a viscous mass. The term **isostasy** was introduced in 1889 by the American geologist **Clarence Dutton**.

A block of crust with a density of 2.7 g/cm³ floats on a mantle of 3.3 g/cm³. If you divide 2.7 by 3.3, you get about 0.82. So about **82 per cent** of the block lies below the surface of the mantle. For a mountain 5 kilometres high, according to Airy, the root works out at 5 times 2.7 divided by 0.6, that is, **22.5 kilometres** deep.

In the 19th century two researchers put forward models. According to **George Airy**, all blocks of crust have about the same density. High mountains therefore reach far into the mantle with a deep **root**, like a big iceberg. According to **John Pratt**, all blocks reach about the same depth, but higher blocks consist of lighter rock with a lower density. In nature both cases occur.

During the last Ice Age an **ice sheet** a kilometre thick lay on Scandinavia and pressed the crust down. When the ice melted, the load disappeared. Since then the land has been slowly rising again, like a boat that is being unloaded. The coast of **Höga Kusten** in Sweden shows the greatest post-glacial uplift of land in the world and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

When a mountain range is worn away by **erosion**, it becomes lighter and slowly rises again. In the Alps too this plays a part, as does the melting of the Ice Age glaciers. Measurements show that parts of the Swiss Alps are rising today by about **1 millimetre a year**. That is little, but in a thousand years it adds up to a whole metre.

gewusst: On the Höga Kusten, old shorelines now lie almost 300 metres above the sea.
If the ice of Greenland melted completely, the land there too would slowly rise.

teile.einleitung: The **Yangtze**, also called the Yangtze Kiang, is the longest river in Asia. It flows right across **China** from the Tibetan Plateau to the sea at Shanghai. In Chinese it is called Chang Jiang, “long river”.
wichtigste: The Yangtze is the longest river in Asia and the third longest in the world.
It rises on the **Tibetan Plateau**.
Its upper course is called the **Jinsha Jiang**.
It flows into the **East China Sea** at Shanghai.
On the Yangtze stands the huge **Three Gorges Dam**, which generates electricity.
Nanjing, a former capital city of China, lies on the lower course.

abschnitte.titel: From the plateau to the sea
abschnitte.text: The Yangtze is about 6,300 kilometres long. Only the Nile and the Amazon are longer, so it takes **third place** among the longest rivers in the world. It rises on the **Tibetan Plateau**. In the mountainous south-west of China its upper course is called the **Jinsha Jiang**, “river of golden sand”. After that it flows east through the whole of China.

On the Yangtze lie many big cities, such as Chongqing and Wuhan. On the lower course lies **Nanjing**, which was the capital city of China several times. At the mouth lies the huge city of **Shanghai**, one of the biggest cities in the world. There the river flows into the **East China Sea**. The river is an important waterway for ships.

In a narrow valley with three gorges, the **Three Gorges Dam** was built. Its power station is the most powerful in the world and generates a great deal of **electricity**. The dam is also meant to prevent floods. For the reservoir, though, over a million people had to move, and many villages and ancient sites went under water. That is why the dam is controversial.

In the valley of the Yangtze lives a large part of the people of China. On the fertile fields a lot of **rice** is grown. The river provides water, fish and transport routes. In the past a special river dolphin, the baiji, lived in the Yangtze. Today it is considered probably extinct.

gewusst: The Yangtze is the longest river in the world that flows through only a single country.
In the catchment area of the Yangtze lives about a third of the population of China.

teile.einleitung: The Iguazú Falls are among the biggest waterfalls in the world. They lie in South America on the border between Argentina and Brazil. Dense rainforest grows around the falls.
wichtigste: The Iguazú Falls lie in South America.
The River Iguazú forms the border between Argentina and Brazil here.
The falls consist of about 275 individual waterfalls.
The edge over which the water drops is about 2.7 kilometres long.
The biggest fall is called the Devil’s Throat.
In the language of the Guaraní, Iguazú means “great water”.

abschnitte.text: The falls lie on the **River Iguazú**, which here forms the border between **Argentina** and **Brazil**. On the Argentine side they belong to the province of **Misiones**, which is named after earlier Jesuit missions. About 20 kilometres after the falls the Iguazú flows into the **Paraná**. There the borders of Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay meet.

The Iguazú Falls are not a single fall. They consist of about **275 individual waterfalls**. These are spread along an edge about **2.7 kilometres** long in the shape of a horseshoe. In between lie small islands with rainforest. Exactly how many falls there are depends on how much water the river is carrying at the time.

The biggest section is called the **Devil’s Throat**, in Spanish “Garganta del Diablo”. It is a U-shaped gorge. There the most water plunges down. On walkways visitors can get very close. The noise is huge, and over the gorge a cloud of fine water droplets rises, in which rainbows often shine.

Dense **rainforest** grows around the falls. Both countries have a **national park** there, and both are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. In the forest live toucans, colourful butterflies and **coatis**. The coatis often come close to visitors, but you should not feed them.

gewusst: The name Iguazú comes from the language of the Guaraní and means “great water”.
The Iguazú Falls are clearly wider than Niagara Falls in North America.

teile.einleitung: The Greenland ice sheet is the huge blanket of ice that covers most of Greenland. It is the second largest mass of ice on Earth. How it changes is very important for the climate and for sea level.
wichtigste: The ice sheet covers about 80 per cent of the area of Greenland.
At its thickest point it is a good 3 kilometres thick.
If it all melted, the sea level would rise by about 7 metres.
Only the Antarctic ice sheet is even bigger.
The Ilulissat Icefjord has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2004.
The Swiss Alfred de Quervain crossed the ice sheet in 1912.

abschnitte.text: The ice sheet covers about **80 per cent** of the area of Greenland. Free of it are mainly the coastal strips, where people also live. At its thickest point the ice is **a good 3 kilometres** thick. Under this enormous weight the rock in the middle of the island is pressed down deeply. The Greenland ice sheet is the **second largest mass of ice** on Earth, and only the **Antarctic ice sheet** is bigger.

The ice of Greenland contains so much water that the **sea level would rise by about 7 metres** if it all melted. A complete melting, however, would take centuries to thousands of years. For some decades the ice sheet has been losing ice every year because of **global warming**. Even today this contributes to the rise in sea level.

On the west coast lies the **Ilulissat Icefjord**. Since **2004** it has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. The glacier **Sermeq Kujalleq** flows into the fjord. It is one of the fastest glaciers in the world. A great many icebergs break off from it and drift through the fjord into the sea.

In **1912** the Swiss geophysicist **Alfred de Quervain** led an expedition across the ice sheet. His team crossed Greenland from west to east. It was one of the first crossings of the island. On the way the researchers collected measurements of the weather and the ice.

Researchers drill deep **ice cores** out of the ice sheet. Tiny **air bubbles** and dust from many thousands of years are trapped in the ice. From these you can read how warm it used to be and what the air was made up of. In this way people learn a great deal about the **climate of the past**. The University of Bern is also involved in this research.

gewusst: The ice is so heavy that the rock in the middle of Greenland is pressed below sea level.
The air bubbles in ice cores are tiny samples of air from many thousands of years ago.

teile.einleitung: A high-pressure area, or high for short, is an area in which the air pressure is higher than in its surroundings. Highs often bring calm, dry weather. In winter, however, in Switzerland they can also bring high fog and the cold Bise.
wichtigste: A high-pressure area is called an anticyclone in technical language.
In the Northern Hemisphere the air in a high circulates clockwise.
An omega block often blocks the path of lows for weeks.
A high in the north and a low in the south often bring Switzerland the cold Bise.
In a winter high, high fog often lies over the Central Plateau below an inversion.
Over Central Asia the powerful Siberian High forms in winter.

abschnitte.text: In a **high-pressure area** the air pressure is higher than in its surroundings. In technical language it is called an **anticyclone**. The air there sinks slowly and warms up as it does so. That is why clouds often dissolve, and the weather is calm and dry. In the Northern Hemisphere the air circulates around a high **clockwise**. The counterpart is the **low-pressure area**, which often brings clouds and rain.

Sometimes a high stays in the same place for a long time. At altitude, the **jet stream**, a strong westerly wind, bends around the high. On the weather map this looks like the Greek letter **omega**. It is called an **omega block**. It blocks the lows that would otherwise bring rain. In this way **heat** or **drought** can last for weeks.

If a high lies north of Switzerland and a low over the Mediterranean, air flows from high to low pressure. Then the **Bise** often blows. It brings cold, dry air from north-eastern Europe to the **Central Plateau**. The Bise usually blows from the **north-east to east**. Between the Jura and the Alps it is squeezed in, and so it becomes particularly strong on Lake Geneva.

In winter a high often brings dull weather to the Central Plateau. Cold, heavy air collects in the lowlands, with warmer air lying above it. This layering is called an **inversion**. At its boundary **high fog** often forms for days. In the mountains above the fog, by contrast, it is sunny and often even mild.

In winter the huge landmass of **Asia** cools down strongly. The cold, heavy air creates a powerful high over Central Asia, the **Siberian High**. It is one of the strongest highs on Earth. It also drives the **winter monsoon** in East Asia, which brings cold, dry air to the south.

gewusst: The highest air pressure on Earth is usually measured in winter in the Siberian High.
In the Southern Hemisphere the air turns around a high exactly the other way, that is, anticlockwise.

teile.einleitung: A dog sled is a sled pulled by several dogs. In the far north it has long been an important means of transport on snow and ice. Today there are also famous dog sled races.
wichtigste: Often huskies or Alaskan malamutes pull the sled.
The person who steers the sled is called a musher.
The dogs together form a team, and the lead dog runs at the very front.
The sled glides on runners over snow and ice.
The famous Iditarod race takes place in Alaska.
In Greenland dog sleds are still important today.

abschnitte.text: Sled dogs are very hardy and love to run. Well known are the **huskies**, which have thick coats and hardly ever feel the cold. The **Alaskan malamute** is bigger and especially strong. It can pull heavy loads. On sharp ice the dogs wear small cloth shoes called **booties**. They protect the paws from injury.

Several dogs are harnessed to the sled with lines. This is called a **team**. The **lead dog** runs at the very front. It listens to the commands and shows the other dogs the way. The sled glides on **runners**, which are long, smooth rails.

The person who steers a dog sled is called a **musher**. They stand at the back on the runners and steer the dogs with calls. A good musher knows each dog well and makes sure that all of them drink, eat and rest enough. After a long run they look after their animals first.

The best-known race is the **Iditarod** in **Alaska**. It runs over about 1,500 kilometres to the town of Nome and usually lasts more than a week. In **Greenland**, the biggest island in the world, dog sleds are still an important means of transport in winter. In the Alps too, for example in Switzerland, sled dog races take place in winter.

gewusst: A good sled dog team can cover well over 100 kilometres in a day.
The Iditarod recalls a journey in 1925 in which dog sleds brought urgently needed medicine to Nome.

teile.einleitung: Cambodia is a kingdom in South-East Asia. The country is famous for the huge temple complex of Angkor Wat and went through a terrible time under the Khmer Rouge.
wichtigste: The capital city of Cambodia is Phnom Penh.
Cambodia borders Thailand, Laos and Vietnam.
The currency is called the riel, and people also often pay with US dollars.
From 1975 to 1979 the Khmer Rouge ruled.
The temple of Angkor Wat is even on the national flag.
The Mekong flows through the country.

abschnitte.text: Cambodia lies in **South-East Asia**. It borders **Thailand**, **Laos** and **Vietnam**. In the south-west lies the Gulf of Thailand. Through the country flows the great river **Mekong**. In the middle lies the **Tonle Sap**, a huge lake that grows greatly in the rainy season. The people speak **Khmer**, and most are Buddhists.

The capital city is **Phnom Penh**. It lies where the Tonle Sap River flows into the Mekong, and is the biggest city in the country. The official currency is the **riel**. In everyday life, though, people often also pay with **US dollars**. Many people work in agriculture, above all in **rice growing**.

Many centuries ago the **Khmer Empire** was very powerful. From that time comes the temple complex of **Angkor Wat**. It is regarded as the biggest religious building in the world and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Angkor Wat is so important for the country that the temple is shown on Cambodia’s **flag**. Every year a great many people visit it.

abschnitte.titel: The time of the Khmer Rouge
abschnitte.text: Cambodia was for a long time a French colony and became independent in **1953**. From **1975 to 1979** the group of the **Khmer Rouge** ruled the country with great harshness. It forced people from the cities to work in the countryside. An estimated **1.5 to 2 million people** died through violence, hunger and forced labour. Today memorials recall this time.

gewusst: Cambodia is one of the few countries that show a building on their flag.
The Tonle Sap is special: in the rainy season its water flows in one direction, and in the dry season in the other.

teile.einleitung: The Hadley cell is a large circulation of air in the tropics. At the equator warm air rises, and in the subtropics it sinks again. The trade winds and the great deserts belong to this circulation.
wichtigste: The Hadley cell is named after George Hadley, who described it in 1735.
At the equator air rises, and in the subtropics it sinks.
At ground level the air flows back to the equator as the trade wind.
The high-altitude flow towards the north or south is called the anti-trade wind.
In the tropics the cell reaches up to about 15 to 18 kilometres.
Towards the poles it is followed by the Ferrel cell.
Deserts such as the Sahara lie in the area of the sinking air.

abschnitte.text: At the **equator** the Sun shines particularly strongly. The warm, damp air rises. High up it flows towards the **subtropics**, that is, to the north and to the south. This high-altitude flow is called the **anti-trade wind**. There the air sinks and flows back to the equator at ground level as the **trade wind**. In this way a circulation forms in each hemisphere, the **Hadley cell**.

The English scholar **George Hadley** described this circulation in **1735**. He explained the trade winds by rising air at the equator and the **rotation of the Earth**. Because of the Earth’s rotation, the trade winds do not blow exactly to the south or north, but at a slant from the east. That is why the circulation cell is named after him. The Hadley cell covers the whole lower layer of air, the **troposphere**. In the tropics it reaches up to about **15 to 18 kilometres**.

The rising air contains a lot of **water vapour**. As it rises it cools, and the vapour **condenses** into clouds. This releases the heat that was stored when the water evaporated. This **latent heat** gives the air extra lift. That is why it often rains heavily at the equator. Because warm air rises and cooler air sinks, the Hadley cell is called a **thermally direct** circulation.

On its way at high altitude the air cools, becomes denser and **sinks** in the subtropics. As it sinks it is compressed and **warms up**. Clouds dissolve as this happens, and it hardly rains.
