It was discovered in **1941** by the geologist **Tatyana Ustinova**. In **2007** a landslide buried part of the springs.

Kamchatka separates the **Sea of Okhotsk** in the west from the **Pacific** and the **Bering Sea** in the east. The most important city is **Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky** on Avacha Bay. It is not connected to the Russian road or rail network. You can reach it only by **aeroplane** or **ship**.

On Kamchatka live a great many **brown bears**. In summer large numbers of **salmon** swim up the rivers. The bears stand in the water and fish them out. In this way they eat themselves fat for the winter. Large parts of the peninsula are wild and hardly settled.

gewusst: The volcanoes of Kamchatka are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Between Kamchatka and Moscow there are several time zones.

teile.einleitung: In the mountains the plant life changes with height. The higher you climb, the colder it gets, and the fewer plants can grow. These bands are called altitudinal zones.
wichtigste: The altitudinal zones in the Alps are called, from bottom to top, colline, montane, subalpine, alpine and nival.
For every 100 metres of height, it gets about 0.6 °C cooler on average.
Most of Switzerland’s vineyards lie in the colline zone.
In the montane zone of the northern Alps, beeches and silver firs grow.
In the subalpine zone, coniferous forests grow up to the tree line.
The highest, nival zone is marked by snow and ice.

abschnitte.text: If you climb 100 metres higher, it gets about **0.6 °C** cooler on average. After 1,000 metres of climbing it is therefore about 6 °C colder. With the cold, the summer also gets shorter. That is why different plants grow higher up than in the valley. On **south-facing slopes** the zones lie higher than on north-facing ones, because the Sun warms them more strongly.

The **colline zone** is the hill zone at low, warm altitudes. Here grow mixed deciduous forests with oaks, fruit trees and **grapevines**. Above it follows the **montane zone**, the mountain zone. In the northern Alps, **beeches** and **silver firs** shape the mixed mountain forests, often mixed with spruces.

In the **subalpine zone** mainly coniferous forests grow, with spruces, larches and the **Swiss stone pine**. The Swiss stone pine, also called the arolla pine, withstands great cold, and its wood smells strongly. At the very top the forest ends at the **tree line**. In the Swiss Alps, depending on the region, it lies roughly between 1,800 and 2,300 metres.

Above the tree line lies the **alpine zone**. It is too cold for trees here. Grassland, dwarf shrubs and many alpine flowers such as the **edelweiss** grow. In summer these areas are used as **alpine pastures**. At the very top follows the **nival zone** with eternal snow and ice. The word comes from the Latin “nix” for snow.

gewusst: The edelweiss protects itself with its felty hairs against strong sunlight, cold and drying out.
Individual flowering plants have been found in the Alps at heights of over 4,000 metres.

teile.einleitung: The Green Revolution was a great change in farming from the 1960s onwards. New varieties of wheat and rice brought much higher harvests. They helped to prevent famines, but were also criticised.
wichtigste: Norman Borlaug is regarded as the “father of the Green Revolution” and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970.
The new high-yield varieties had short, sturdy stalks.
The rice variety IR8 became known as “miracle rice” in 1966.
The International Rice Research Institute, IRRI, has its seat in the Philippines.
The Punjab in India is regarded as a prime example for wheat.
The varieties needed artificial fertiliser, irrigation and pesticides.
The term was coined in 1968 by William Gaud.

abschnitte.text: The American agricultural scientist **Norman Borlaug** worked from 1944 in a programme of the Rockefeller Foundation in **Mexico**. There he bred high-yield wheat varieties that were resistant to diseases. His varieties helped to prevent famines in Mexico, India and Pakistan. For this he received the **Nobel Peace Prize in 1970**. His work led in 1966 to the research centre **CIMMYT** near Mexico City.

The secret of the new **high-yield varieties** was **short, sturdy stalks**. Old varieties with long stalks bent over when the ears became too heavy. The new, semi-dwarf varieties stayed upright. This way they could turn a lot of fertiliser into grain. In rice, the variety **IR8** became famous, which appeared in 1966 and was regarded as “miracle rice”. It comes from the **International Rice Research Institute, IRRI**, which was founded in 1960 in Los Baños in the **Philippines**.

A prime example is the Indian state of **Punjab**. There, from the mid-1960s, new wheat varieties, fertiliser and wells were introduced especially quickly. The Punjab became the **breadbasket of India**. India could in this way grow much more grain itself. The name “Green Revolution” was coined in **1968** by the US official **William Gaud**, head of the development agency USAID.

The new varieties only gave top yields if they were properly looked after. They needed a lot of **artificial fertiliser**, reliable **irrigation** and **pesticides** against pests. This package was expensive. Without water and fertiliser, the new varieties were often no better than the old ones.

The Green Revolution helped to feed many millions of people. But it is also criticised. **Larger farms** with money and land often benefited more than poor **smallholders**. As a result, the gaps between rich and poor grew in some regions. In addition, a lot of fertiliser, pesticides and irrigation led in some places to problems with soils and groundwater. Experts still discuss how to combine high harvests with protecting the environment.

gewusst: Norman Borlaug is one of the few agricultural scientists to have received the Nobel Peace Prize.
The name “Green Revolution” was meant to set a peaceful change apart from a political revolution.

teile.einleitung: K2 is the second highest mountain on Earth. It stands in the Karakoram on the border between Pakistan and China and is considered one of the most difficult mountains for climbers.
wichtigste: K2 is about 8,611 metres high.
Only Mount Everest is higher.
It is the highest mountain in the Karakoram.
The border between Pakistan and China runs over its summit.
Italians were the first to climb it, on 31 July 1954.
In January 2021 ten climbers from Nepal succeeded in the first winter ascent.

abschnitte.text: K2 lies in the **Karakoram**, a separate high mountain range north-west of the Himalayas. The border between **Pakistan** and **China** runs over the summit. Around the mountain there are huge glaciers. Most expeditions start from the Pakistani side. The journey to the foot of the mountain alone takes several days.

The name K2 sounds like a code, and that is what it is. In 1856 a British **surveyor** numbered the peaks in the Karakoram K1, K2 and so on. K stands for Karakoram, and the 2 for the number. For many other mountains, local names later came into use. With K2 the survey number simply stayed.

For a long time climbers did not make it all the way to the top. On **31 July 1954** **Achille Compagnoni** and **Lino Lacedelli** reached the summit. They belonged to an **Italian expedition**. This was a year after the first ascent of Mount Everest. The success was greatly celebrated in Italy.

Climbers call K2 the **“Savage Mountain”**. Its slopes are very steep, and there are avalanches and rockfall. The **weather** can suddenly change, with storms and great cold. Many climbers have died on K2. That is why it is considered more dangerous than Mount Everest.

In winter it is even colder and stormier on K2. For a long time it was the last **eight-thousander** without a winter ascent. On **16 January 2021** ten climbers from **Nepal** reached the summit together. Among them was **Nirmal Purja**. The group walked the last metres together, so that all arrived at the top at the same time.

gewusst: K2 is only a good 200 metres lower than Mount Everest.
Eight-thousanders are all the mountains that are over 8,000 metres high. There are exactly 14 of them on Earth.

teile.einleitung: A capital city is the most important city of a country, and usually the government and parliament sit there. Often it is also the biggest city, but not always. Switzerland is a special case: Bern is the seat of the government, but is officially called the federal city.
wichtigste: A capital is usually the seat of the government and parliament of a country.
The Swiss government, the Federal Council, has its seat in Bern.
The capital of Austria is Vienna.
The capital of Spain is Madrid.
The capital of Japan is Tokyo.
The capital is not always the biggest city of a country.
Cantons also have a main town, for example Zurich, Lausanne or Chur.

abschnitte.text: A **capital city** is the city in which the most important authorities of a country have their seat. There the **government**, the parliament and often the head of state usually work. Many embassies of other countries are also in the capital. Often the capital is also the cultural and economic centre.

In Switzerland, the constitution nowhere says that Bern is the capital. Bern was chosen in 1848 as the seat of the Federal Council and parliament and is officially called the **federal city**. In the **Federal Palace** the National Council and the Council of States meet. The biggest city in Switzerland, however, is Zurich.

The capital of Austria is **Vienna**, that of Spain is **Madrid** and that of Japan is **Tokyo**. The Greater Tokyo area is one of the biggest urban areas in the world, with over 35 million people. Other examples are Paris in France, Berlin in Germany and Rome in Italy. Washington is the capital of the USA, although New York is much bigger.

Some capitals were newly built so that there would be no quarrel between big cities. **Canberra** in Australia was laid out between Sydney and Melbourne. **Brasília** was planned in the middle of the interior of Brazil and was inaugurated in 1960. Ottawa in Canada was also chosen as a compromise.

In some countries the capital and the seat of government are separate. In the Netherlands, **Amsterdam** is the capital, but the government and parliament sit in **The Hague**. Bolivia has Sucre as its constitutional capital, while the government works in La Paz. Some countries have also moved their capital, for example Germany from Bonn to Berlin.

Every Swiss canton also has a **main town**, in which the cantonal government and cantonal parliament meet. Examples are Zurich, Bern, Lucerne, Geneva, Sion in Valais and Bellinzona in Ticino. The main town of the Grisons is Chur, and that of Appenzell Inner Rhodes is called Appenzell. Some main towns are quite small, such as Altdorf in the canton of Uri.

begriffe.erklaerung: The city in which the government of a country has its seat.
The official name for Bern as the seat of the Federal Council and parliament.
The place where the government works.
The official representation of one country in another country.

gewusst: Switzerland is one of the few countries that officially have no capital city.
Reykjavík in Iceland is the northernmost capital of an independent state.

teile.einleitung: Coffee is one of the most popular drinks in the world. It is made from the roasted beans of the coffee plant, which grows only in warm countries around the equator.
wichtigste: Coffee beans are the seeds inside the red coffee cherries.
Raw beans are greenish, and only when roasted do they turn brown.
The coffee plant comes from Ethiopia in Africa.
Coffee grows in the coffee belt of the tropics.
Brazil harvests the most coffee, and Vietnam is in second place.
The caffeine in coffee keeps you awake.

abschnitte.titel: From the shrub to the bean
abschnitte.text: Coffee grows on a **shrub** with glossy leaves. Its fruits are red and look like small cherries, which is why they are called **coffee cherries**. In each fruit there are usually two seeds: the **coffee beans**. Raw, they are greenish and have hardly any scent. Only when **roasted** do they turn brown and get their typical aroma. After that they are ground.

The home of **Arabica coffee** is the highlands of **Ethiopia**. From there it came via Arabia into the whole world. Coffee needs warmth and a lot of rain and cannot stand frost. It therefore grows in the **coffee belt** between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn. The biggest coffee country is **Brazil**. In second place comes **Vietnam** (as of 2024).

There are two important kinds of coffee. **Arabica** tastes mild and likes to grow in the highlands. **Robusta** is stronger and more bitter and contains more caffeine. Vietnam grows mainly Robusta. Many coffee blends consist of both kinds. An **espresso** is a small, strong coffee from Italy that is made with hot water under high pressure.

Coffee contains **caffeine**. This substance acts on the nervous system and makes tired people alert again. Too much caffeine, though, can make you restless and disturb your sleep. That is why coffee is not for children. Caffeine is also found, by the way, in tea, cola and some energy drinks.

No coffee grows in Switzerland, because it is too cold. Even so, the country plays a big part: many large **coffee trading firms** have their headquarters here. The Swiss firm **Nestlé** brought the instant coffee **Nescafé** onto the market in 1938. Later, coffee capsules were added. In many Swiss households today there is a coffee machine.

gewusst: A legend tells that a herdsman in Ethiopia discovered coffee because his goats skipped around especially lively after eating the fruits.
Brazil harvests almost a third of the coffee of the whole world.

teile.einleitung: Sharks are fish that have lived in the seas for a very long time. There are many species, from the giant whale shark to small sharks of less than a metre. Many people fear them, although attacks on people are very rare.
wichtigste: Sharks are fish with a skeleton made of cartilage instead of bone.
The whale shark is the biggest fish in the world and can grow over 12 metres long.
The whale shark eats mainly tiny plankton and is harmless to people.
The hammerhead shark gets its name from its broad head.
Sharks have a very good sense of smell.
Sharks have existed for over 400 million years, so even before the dinosaurs.
Sharks very rarely attack people.

abschnitte.text: Sharks are fish. Unlike most fish, though, they do not have a skeleton made of bone, but of **cartilage**. Cartilage is firmer than flesh but more flexible than bone. You have cartilage too, for example in your ears and the tip of your nose. Many sharks have several rows of teeth. If a tooth falls out, a new one moves up.

The **whale shark** is the biggest fish in the world. It can grow over 12 metres long. Despite its size it eats mainly **plankton**, which are tiny living things in the water. It swims with its mouth open and filters them out. The whale shark is harmless to people. Divers can even swim next to it.

There are several hundred species of shark. The **hammerhead shark** has a head as broad as a hammer. The eyes sit at its two ends. Also well known is the **great white shark**, a big hunter. Many other sharks are small and live on the seabed. Every species is adapted to its habitat.

Sharks have very good senses. Their **sense of smell** in particular is fine: they notice even the smallest traces in the water. They also feel movements in the water through sensory cells on the sides of their bodies. With special organs on their heads they even pick up weak electrical signals sent out by other animals.

Sharks have existed for over **400 million years**. The first dinosaurs only lived much later. Today many species of shark are **threatened**. People catch very many sharks every year, often for their fins. Attacks by sharks on people, on the other hand, are very rare. Much more often it is the other way round: humans are dangerous for sharks.

gewusst: Sharks existed before there were trees on Earth.
A shark can lose thousands of teeth in the course of its life, because new ones always grow back.

teile.einleitung: Ibn Battuta was a traveller from Morocco who lived in the 14th century. In about 30 years he travelled through Africa, Arabia, Asia and as far as China. His account of his travels is still an important source about the world of his time.
wichtigste: Ibn Battuta was born in 1304 in Tangier in present-day Morocco.
In 1325 he set out on a pilgrimage to Mecca.
In all he covered about 120,000 kilometres, more than Marco Polo.
In Delhi and on the Maldives he worked as a judge.
On his last journey he visited the Mali Empire in West Africa.
His travel account is called the Rihla, which means “journey”.

abschnitte.text: Ibn Battuta was born in **1304** in **Tangier**. He studied Islamic law. At the age of 21, in 1325, he set out on the **Hajj**, the pilgrimage to **Mecca**. But after the pilgrimage he did not go back home. He travelled on for almost 30 years through the world as it was then known.

Because Ibn Battuta was a **legal scholar**, he found work on the way. The Sultan of **Delhi** appointed him for several years as a **qadi**, that is, a judge. Later he also served as a qadi on the **Maldives** in the Indian Ocean for about nine months. In this way he got to know many rulers and cultures.

By sea, according to his account, Ibn Battuta reached **China**. He landed in the port city of **Quanzhou** and travelled as far as Hangzhou. Whether he also got as far as Beijing, as he claimed, is doubted by researchers. In all he covered about **120,000 kilometres**. That is more than Marco Polo and three times around the Earth.

On his last great journey he crossed the **Sahara** in 1352 and 1353. He visited the rich **Mali Empire** in West Africa, to which the city of **Timbuktu** also belonged. After that he returned to Morocco for good.

After his return Ibn Battuta dictated his experiences to the scholar **Ibn Juzayy**. This is how the travel account **Rihla** came about, Arabic for “journey”. It tells of cities, markets, rulers and customs of many countries. Historians still use it today, even if not every detail is accurate.

gewusst: A crater on the Moon is named after Ibn Battuta.
In Dubai there is a big shopping centre named after Ibn Battuta that shows the countries he travelled in.

teile.einleitung: Mount Cameroon is an active volcano in the West African country of Cameroon. It is the highest mountain in West Africa and rises almost directly from the Atlantic.
wichtigste: Mount Cameroon is a good 4,000 metres high.
It is the highest mountain in West Africa.
It is an active volcano, most recently with larger eruptions in 1999 and 2000.
Its local name “Mongo ma Ndemi” means Mountain of Greatness.
On its south-west slopes it rains extremely heavily.
The town of Buea lies on the slope.

abschnitte.text: Mount Cameroon is a **volcano** that erupts again and again. There were larger eruptions, for example, in **1999** and **2000**. Streams of lava flowed down the slopes. Depending on the measurement, its height is given as **4,040 to 4,095 metres**. This makes it the **highest mountain in West Africa**. It is somewhat lower than the Matterhorn at 4,478 metres. The highest mountain in the whole of Africa is Kilimanjaro.

The mountain rises almost directly from the coast of the **Gulf of Guinea**, which belongs to the **Atlantic**. That is why it can be seen well from the sea. Damp sea air flows against the mountain, rises and rains out. On the **south-west slopes**, in some places over 10,000 millimetres of rain fall a year. They are among the **rainiest places on Earth**.

On the mountain live the **Bakweri**. They call it **“Mongo ma Ndemi”**, which means Mountain of Greatness. At a height of about 900 metres lies the town of **Buea**. It is the capital of a region of Cameroon. Many ascents start from there. The fertile volcanic soils are used for agriculture.

Around **470 BC** the navigator **Hanno** from Carthage sailed along the coast of West Africa. In his account of the journey he describes a fire-spouting mountain. He calls it in Greek “Theon Ochema”, which means **Chariot of the Gods**. Usually this mountain is identified with Mount Cameroon. Probably Hanno witnessed an eruption.

gewusst: Every year a mountain race takes place on Mount Cameroon in which runners race to the summit and back.
Mount Cameroon is the highest point of the whole country of Cameroon.

teile.einleitung: Hail is made up of pellets of ice that fall from the sky. It forms in big thunderclouds and can cause great damage in a short time. In Switzerland it hails mainly in summer.
wichtigste: Hail consists of ice pellets that fall from thunderclouds.
A single piece is called a hailstone.
Hailstones are at least 5 millimetres across, and smaller pellets are called graupel.
In Switzerland it hails most often in summer, because that is when most thunderstorms happen.
Large hail can damage cars, roofs, fields and gardens.
Hail nets protect fruit trees from hail.
In hail you are best protected in a house or car.

abschnitte.text: Hail forms in tall **thunderclouds**. Inside them there are strong updrafts that carry drops of water far upwards. Up there it is so cold that the drops freeze. The small ice pellets are whirled up and down several times and grow as they do so, because new water freezes onto them. When they become too heavy, they fall to the ground as hail.

The individual pieces of ice are called **hailstones**. Only from a diameter of **5 millimetres** do people speak of hail. Smaller, soft pellets are called **graupel**. Many hailstones are about as big as peas. In very strong thunderstorms, though, they can grow as big as table tennis balls or even bigger.

In Switzerland it hails mainly in **summer**. Then the air is warm and damp, and many thunderstorms form. Hail usually falls only in a narrow strip and often lasts only a few minutes. Even so, it can cause great damage to cars, houses and fields. Many people therefore take out insurance against hail damage.

The hard ice pellets hit leaves, blossoms and fruit. Plants in the garden can be torn to shreds, and whole harvests can be lost. Many farmers therefore stretch **hail nets** over their fruit trees. The nets catch the pellets before they hit the fruit. Vineyards are sometimes protected in this way too.

Large hailstones are hard and heavy and can hurt. When a hailstorm comes, it is best to go **into a house**. In a car you are protected too. Cars should be put in a garage if possible. Weather services often warn in advance of strong thunderstorms with hail.

gewusst: A hailstone can have layers inside like an onion, because it was whirled up and down several times in the cloud.
After a hailstorm the ground can look white for a short time as after a snowfall, even in the middle of summer.

teile.einleitung: The coordinate grid (or graticule) is an imaginary network of lines laid over the whole Earth. With it, you can give any place exactly with two numbers: its latitude and its longitude.
wichtigste: Lines of latitude run parallel to the equator, and meridians join the North and South Poles.
Latitude is counted from the equator up to 90° north or 90° south.
Longitude is counted from the prime meridian up to 180° east or 180° west.
One degree has 60 arcminutes, and one arcminute has 60 arcseconds.
In the north-south direction, one degree of latitude is equal to about 111 kilometres.
The prime meridian runs through the observatory at Greenwich near London.
Bern lies at just under 47° north and a good 7° east.

abschnitte.text: The **lines of latitude** run like rings around the Earth, parallel to the **equator**. The equator has a latitude of 0°, and the poles lie at 90° north and 90° south. The **meridians** are half circles from pole to pole. They are counted starting from the **prime meridian**, going 180° to the east and 180° to the west. At intervals of one degree there are 360 meridians, because 180° east and 180° west are the same meridian.

One degree is divided into 60 **arcminutes**, and each arcminute into 60 **arcseconds**. So one degree has 3600 arcseconds. The circumference of the Earth over the poles measures about 40,000 kilometres. If you divide that by 360, you get about 111 kilometres per degree of latitude. One arcminute along a meridian is about 1.85 kilometres long. This is exactly why the **nautical mile** is fixed at 1852 metres.

Every place gets two **coordinates**: first the latitude, then the longitude. Bern, for example, lies at about 46.9° N and 7.4° E, while Berlin is at about 52.5° N and 13.4° E. The **antipode** of a place lies exactly on the opposite side of the globe. For it, the latitude changes to the other hemisphere, and the longitude is 180° minus the original longitude, with east becoming west. The antipode of 47° N, 8° E therefore lies at 47° S, 172° W in the Pacific.

The Earth turns once through 360° in 24 hours. That is **15° per hour**. So longitude and the time of day are connected. If two places are 15 degrees of longitude apart, their **mean local time** differs by one hour. A place at 45° E and one at 30° W are 75° apart, which gives a difference of 5 hours. Today’s time zones are based on this calculation, but they often follow national borders.

In the past many countries had their own prime meridian. In October 1884 delegates met in Washington for the **International Meridian Conference**. They voted for the meridian through the **Greenwich observatory** as the common prime meridian. France abstained and went on using the Paris meridian for decades. Today maps, ships and navigation devices all over the world use Greenwich as the starting point.

gewusst: The nautical mile is no coincidence: it is almost exactly one arcminute on a meridian.
The antipode of Switzerland lies in the middle of the Pacific, south-east of New Zealand.

teile.einleitung: A harbour is a sheltered place by the water where ships can moor. Goods are loaded and unloaded there, and people get on and off. Switzerland has harbours too, although it does not lie on the sea.
wichtigste: Rotterdam in the Netherlands is the biggest harbour in Europe.
In Basel there are Rhine harbours for cargo ships.
Lighthouses show ships the way along the coast at night.
Tugs pull and push big ships in the harbour.
Pilots help the captain to sail safely into the harbour.

abschnitte.text: A **harbour** is a place on the sea, on a lake or on a river where ships can moor safely. Often long walls, the **moles**, protect the harbour from waves. At the **quays**, goods are loaded and unloaded. Big **cranes** lift containers from the ships onto lorries and trains. There are also harbours for ferries, fishing boats or sailing ships.

The biggest harbour in Europe is **Rotterdam** in the Netherlands. It lies on the **North Sea**, where the Rhine flows into the sea. Huge container ships from all over the world dock there. Many goods that are sold in Europe come through Rotterdam. From there they are carried on by ships on the Rhine, by trains and by lorries.

Switzerland also has harbours for cargo ships. In **Basel**, and right next to it in **Birsfelden** and **Muttenz**, lie the **Rhine harbours**. Here ships arrive that have sailed up the Rhine from the sea. They bring, for example, fuel, grain and containers. Through the Rhine, Switzerland is thus connected to the sea. On the Swiss lakes there are also many small harbours for passenger boats and boats.

On coasts and at harbour entrances stand **lighthouses**. Their bright light shows ships the way at night and warns of dangerous places. Every lighthouse flashes in its own rhythm, which is how you recognise it. Before a big ship sails into the harbour, a **pilot** often comes on board. He knows the harbour and its dangers very well and advises the captain.

Big ships find it hard to turn and brake in a narrow harbour. That is why **tugs** help them. These are small but very strong boats. They pull and push the big ships when they **moor** and **cast off**. Often several tugs work on a single ship at the same time.

gewusst: Through the Rhine harbours in Basel, Switzerland is connected to the sea by ship.
A tug is much smaller than the ships it pulls, but it has a very powerful engine.

teile.einleitung: The Indus is one of the great rivers of Asia. It rises in Tibet and flows through Pakistan to the Arabian Sea. On its banks, about 4,500 years ago, one of the oldest great civilisations in the world arose.
wichtigste: The Indus rises in Tibet and flows briefly through India.
It covers the greatest part of its course in Pakistan.
It is the longest river in Pakistan.
Near Karachi it flows into the Arabian Sea in a delta.
On the Indus the Harappan civilisation arose, with cities such as Mohenjo-Daro.
India takes its name from the River Indus.

abschnitte.text: The Indus **rises** on the plateau of **Tibet**. It flows first through the mountains, then briefly through India and finally through the whole of **Pakistan**. It is the **longest river in Pakistan**. Near the city of **Karachi** it flows into the **Arabian Sea**. There it forms a large **delta**.

Large parts of Pakistan are very dry. The water of the Indus is therefore led through many canals onto the fields. This is called **irrigation**. In this way wheat, rice and cotton can grow. In the north-east lies the region of **Punjab**. Its name means “five waters” or “five rivers”, meaning five tributaries of the Indus.

About **4,500 years ago** the **Harappan civilisation**, also called the **Indus civilisation**, arose on the Indus. It is one of the oldest great civilisations in the world, like those in Egypt and Mesopotamia. The people built large, carefully planned cities. Well known are **Harappa** and **Mohenjo-Daro** in present-day Pakistan.

**Mohenjo-Daro** was a surprisingly modern city. It had straight streets, houses made of baked bricks and **drainage channels**. There was even a large public **bath**. Today the ruins are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Nobody has been able to decipher the script of the Indus civilisation to this day.

The ancient **Greeks** called the land along the River Indus “India”. In this way the name of the river became the name of a whole country. The word “Hindu” is also connected with the old name of the river.

gewusst: In the Indus lives a rare, almost blind species of dolphin, the Indus river dolphin.
The Indus is about two and a half times as long as the Rhine.

teile.einleitung: An island is a piece of land that is surrounded by water on all sides. There are tiny islands with just a few trees on them, and huge ones like Greenland, the biggest island in the world. There are islands in Swiss lakes and rivers too.
wichtigste: An island is land that is surrounded by water on all sides.
The biggest island in the world is Greenland.
Madagascar is a large island off the east coast of Africa.
Sicily belongs to Italy and is the biggest island in the Mediterranean.
Several islands together are called an island group or archipelago.
Islands can form through volcanoes, through corals or by being cut off from the mainland.
On islands there often live animals and plants that occur nowhere else.

abschnitte.text: An **island** is an area of land that is completely surrounded by water, whether by a sea, a lake or a river. If a piece of land is surrounded by water on only three sides, it is called a **peninsula**, like Italy. Several islands lying close together form an **island group** or an archipelago. Australia is surrounded by water, but is counted as a continent.

Some islands used to be joined to the mainland and were cut off by the sea, like Great Britain. **Volcanic islands** such as Hawaii or Iceland form when lava rises from the sea floor and hardens. In warm seas, tiny corals build up reefs over thousands of years, and from these come **coral islands** and ring-shaped atolls. In rivers, islands form from deposited sand and gravel.

**Greenland**, at over 2 million square kilometres, is the biggest island in the world, about fifty times as big as Switzerland. **Madagascar** lies off the east coast of Africa and is the fourth largest island on Earth. **Sicily** belongs to Italy and is the biggest island in the Mediterranean, and the volcano Etna stands there. Indonesia consists of over 17,000 islands and is the biggest island state in the world.

Because islands are cut off, unique animals and plants often develop there. Species that occur in only one place are called **endemic**. On Madagascar, for example, live the lemurs, and on the Galápagos Islands giant tortoises. The naturalist Charles Darwin observed finches there and developed from them ideas for his theory of evolution.

Switzerland has islands too, although it is not on the sea. In Lake Zurich lie the islands of **Ufenau** and Lützelau. In Lake Maggiore the Brissago Islands belong to Ticino, and on one of them grows a botanical garden with plants from all over the world. In Lake Biel lies St Peter’s Island, which today is joined to the shore by a strip of land.

Islanders often depend on ships and aeroplanes to receive goods and visitors. Many islands live from **tourism** and fishing. Low islands such as the Maldives are threatened by rising sea levels. Islands also play a part in many stories, for example as a place for treasure hunts or adventures.

begriffe.erklaerung: Land that is surrounded by water on three sides.
A group of islands lying close together.
A ring-shaped coral island with a lagoon in the middle.
A species that occurs only in one particular place in the world.

gewusst: The island of Surtsey off Iceland came into being only from 1963, through a volcanic eruption in the sea.
Greenland means “green land” when translated, although most of the island is covered with ice.

teile.einleitung: Around the equator there is a belt in which the winds flow together and it rains almost every day. This belt is called the **Intertropical Convergence Zone**, ITCZ for short. It moves north and south in the course of the year and so determines the rainy seasons in the tropics.
wichtigste: In the ITCZ the trade winds of the Northern and Southern Hemispheres meet.
The warm, damp air rises, cools and forms tall thunderclouds.
Typical are heavy afternoon downpours, the zenithal rains.
The ITCZ follows the Sun’s zenith with a delay: in July it lies further north, and in January further south.
On average over the year it lies a little north of the equator, at about 5 degrees north.
Sailors called the zone with little wind the **doldrums**.

abschnitte.text: **Convergence** means flowing together. In both hemispheres the **trade winds** blow from the subtropics towards the equator. In the ITCZ they meet. Because the air cannot move aside, it is pushed upwards. This forms a band of rising air that runs once around the whole Earth.

Over the equator the air is very warm and damp. When it rises, it cools, and the water vapour turns into tiny droplets. Mighty heaped clouds form, called **cumulonimbus**. In the afternoon they often discharge in powerful thunderstorms. These rainfalls are called **zenithal rain**, because they fall where the Sun stands almost vertically at midday.

abschnitte.titel: The zone moves with the Sun
abschnitte.text: The ITCZ follows, with some delay, the region where the Sun is at its **zenith** at midday, that is, vertically overhead. In the northern summer it therefore lies north of the equator, and in the southern summer south of it. Because the Northern Hemisphere has more land and warms up more strongly, on average over the year it lies slightly in the north. Over South Asia it moves especially far in summer, to over 20 degrees north.

Where the ITCZ lies at the moment, it is **rainy season**. In the African **Sahel** it therefore rains only in the northern summer, when the zone moves north. When it withdraws, a long dry season begins. Places near the equator often have two rainy seasons a year, because the ITCZ passes over them twice: once on its way north, and once on its way south.

In the ITCZ the air rises mainly upwards. Horizontal winds are therefore often weak. For sailing ships this was a problem: they sometimes lay becalmed for days in the **doldrums**. The sailors feared these calms, because drinking water and supplies could run short.

gewusst: On satellite pictures the ITCZ can often be seen as a bright band of cloud around the Earth.
The monsoon in India is closely linked to the ITCZ moving far to the north.

teile.einleitung: **Isabela** is the biggest island of the **Galápagos Islands**, which belong to Ecuador in the Pacific. It has grown together from several volcanoes and is still volcanically active today. Special animals live on the island, such as giant tortoises.
wichtigste: Isabela is the biggest of the Galápagos Islands.
The islands belong to Ecuador.
Isabela consists of several **shield volcanoes** that have grown together.
The equator runs across the island.
Galápagos giant tortoises live on Isabela.

abschnitte.text: Isabela was formed from several large **shield volcanoes** that grew together over time into one island. Shield volcanoes have flat, broad slopes because their lava is runny. Some of these volcanoes, such as **Sierra Negra** and **Wolf**, have erupted in recent decades. The volcano Wolf is the highest mountain in the Galápagos Islands.

On Isabela live **giant tortoises**, which can live to a very great age. Because the volcanoes are separated by lava fields, separate forms have developed on different volcanoes. On the coasts you can see marine iguanas, sea lions and Galápagos penguins. These penguins are the only ones that live so close to the equator. Most parts of the island belong to the national park.

The **equator** runs across the north of the island. Isabela is the biggest island, but only a few people live there. The most important place is the fishing village of **Puerto Villamil** on the south coast. Because of its shape, the island reminds some people of a seahorse.

gewusst: At about 4,600 square kilometres, Isabela is bigger than all the other Galápagos Islands put together.
Galápagos penguins are the only species of penguin that also live north of the equator.

teile.einleitung: The Great Barrier Reef is the largest coral reef on Earth. It lies off the north-east coast of Australia and is full of life. Today, however, it is badly threatened by sea water that is too warm.
wichtigste: The reef lies off the coast of the Australian state of Queensland.
It stretches along the coast for about 2300 kilometres.
It consists of about 2900 individual reefs and many small islands.
Its area is about eight times the size of Switzerland.
It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1981.
Sea water that is too warm is the biggest danger today.

abschnitte.titel: A reef made of many reefs
abschnitte.text: A **reef** is a ridge of rock or coral in the sea. The Great Barrier Reef is not a single reef, but consists of about **2900 individual reefs** and many small islands. Together they stretch over about **2300 kilometres**. The area is about 344,000 square kilometres in size, while Switzerland has about 41,000. So the reef is about **eight times as big** as Switzerland.

Corals look like plants or stones, but they are **animals**. Tiny coral polyps build themselves skeletons of limestone. Over thousands of years these grow into huge reefs. In the corals live tiny algae, which give them food and colour. In the reef live countless fish, turtles, mussels and sharks.

Every year **humpback whales** come from the cold seas in the south to the warm reef. There they give birth to their young. On seagrass meadows in the shallow water the **dugong**, a sea cow, feeds. Sea turtles also lay their eggs on the beaches of the islands. Many of these animals are protected.

If the sea water becomes **too warm**, the corals push out their algae and turn white. This is called **coral bleaching**. If it stays warm for a long time, the corals die. On the Great Barrier Reef this has already happened often in recent decades. The **crown-of-thorns starfish** also harms the reef, because it eats corals. When there are very many of them, they destroy large areas.

Since **1981** the reef has been on the list of **UNESCO World Heritage Sites**. A large part of it belongs to a marine park. A well-known starting point for trips is the city of **Cairns** in the north-east of Australia. From there many boats travel to the reef. When snorkelling and diving, you should not touch the corals.

gewusst: The Great Barrier Reef is the largest structure built by living things on Earth.
You can even see the reef from space.

teile.einleitung: A cold desert is a desert in which it is not hot but very cold. Whether an area is a desert depends not on heat, but on how little precipitation falls.
wichtigste: A desert is an area with very little precipitation.
Usually people speak of a desert when less than about 250 millimetres fall in a year.
At about 14 million km², Antarctica is the biggest desert on Earth.
The Arctic is the second biggest desert.
Cold air contains little water vapour, so it hardly ever snows.
In the ice-free areas of Antarctica mainly mosses and lichens grow.

abschnitte.text: When they think of a desert, many people think of sand and heat. What matters, though, is the **precipitation**, that is, rain or snow. If less than about **250 millimetres** fall in a year, an area usually counts as a desert. In Zurich about four times as much falls. A desert can therefore also be icy cold. Then it is called a **cold desert**.

abschnitte.titel: The biggest desert in the world
abschnitte.text: **Antarctica** is about 14 million km² in size and so the biggest desert on Earth, bigger than any hot desert. Although there is so much ice there, only very little snow falls. The ice has built up over **hundreds of thousands of years**, because hardly anything melts. The **Arctic** around the North Pole also receives very little precipitation. At almost 14 million km² it is the second biggest desert.

The colder the air is, the less **water vapour** it can take up. Without water vapour hardly any clouds, rain or snow form. That is why in cold deserts it is not only cold, but also very dry. The wind often blows the little snow back and forth, so that you think it is snowing a lot.

In Antarctica there are even valleys almost without ice and snow: the **McMurdo Dry Valleys**. They are among the driest places on Earth. In the few ice-free areas mainly **mosses** and **lichens** grow, which can withstand cold and dryness. Larger animals such as penguins and seals live on the coasts, because they find their food in the sea.

gewusst: The Sahara is the biggest hot desert, but clearly smaller than Antarctica.
Researchers study the McMurdo Dry Valleys because in some ways they resemble conditions on Mars.

teile.einleitung: **Jordan** is a kingdom in the **Middle East**. A large part of the country is desert, but there are famous ancient sites such as the rock city of Petra. The capital city is **Amman**.
wichtigste: The capital city of Jordan is Amman.
Jordan is a **kingdom**.
Its only access to the sea is at **Aqaba** on the Red Sea.
In the west the **River Jordan** forms the border.
In the south lies the **Wadi Rum** desert with red rocks.
In the north stands the Roman ruined city of **Jerash**.

abschnitte.text: Jordan is ruled by a **king** who comes from the Hashemite family. The country also has a parliament, but the king has a lot of power. Jordan lies between Israel, Syria, Iraq and Saudi Arabia. Most people speak Arabic and are Muslims. The capital city, **Amman**, is built on many hills.

A large part of Jordan is **desert**. In the south lies **Wadi Rum** with red sandstone rocks and wide stretches of sand. Many films have been shot there. Water is scarce all over the country. In the west flows the **River Jordan**, which gave the country its name. It flows into the **Dead Sea**, whose shore is the lowest place on land on Earth.

Jordan has only a short coast. There lies the town of **Aqaba** on the **Red Sea**, with the country’s only port. Through it many goods come into the country. In the warm water off Aqaba there are coral reefs that attract divers.

Very famous is **Petra**, a city that the people of the Nabataeans carved into the rose-red rocks about 2,000 years ago. Petra is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In the north lies **Jerash**, one of the best preserved Roman cities, with colonnaded streets and theatres. From **Mount Nebo**, according to the Bible, Moses saw the Promised Land.

gewusst: In 2007 Petra was chosen as one of the “New Seven Wonders of the World”.
The Swiss explorer Johann Ludwig Burckhardt made Petra known in Europe in 1812.

teile.einleitung: The guanaco is a wild camel from South America. It has no hump and lives in herds in the Andes and the steppes of Patagonia. The llama descends from it.
wichtigste: The guanaco belongs to the camel family but has no hump.
It is the typical large animal of the Patagonian steppe.
It also lives in the Andes and on Tierra del Fuego.
It is adapted to cold, wind and scanty food.
The llama is the domesticated form of the guanaco.

abschnitte.text: The guanaco belongs to the **camels**, like the dromedary and the Bactrian camel. But it has no hump. It has long legs, a long neck and a thick, brown coat with a light belly. Guanacos live wild in South America, from the highlands of the **Andes** to **Tierra del Fuego**. The **llama** descends from the guanaco. It was tamed by people in the Andes thousands of years ago.

The guanaco is especially typical of the steppes of **Patagonia**. There it is cold, windy and dry. The guanaco eats grasses and shrubs and manages with **scanty food**. Its thick coat protects it from cold and wind. Guanacos live in **herds**. When they are disturbed, they warn the others with a shrill call and quickly run away.

The guanaco’s most important natural enemy is the **puma**. In the past, guanacos were also hunted heavily, and in many places they became rare. In national parks such as Torres del Paine in Chile they are now protected and easy to watch. Like llamas, guanacos can also **spit** when they are annoyed.

gewusst: The llama is a tamed guanaco.
Guanacos are related to the camels in Africa and Asia.
